subtopic: TWENTY-FIFTH ANNIVERSARY OF ESTABLISHMENT OF THE RUSSIAN ARMY-TRIBUTE TO ITS VALOUR AND SPIRIT

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: TWENTY-FIFTH ANNIVERSARY OF ESTABLISHMENT OF THE RUSSIAN ARMY-TRIBUTE TO ITS VALOUR AND SPIRIT
speechtext:
To-day marks the celebration in the Soviet Union of the twenty-fifth anniversary of the establishment of the red army. Its achievements in the last twenty months have given to all the free peoples who have been resisting nazi aggression so much cause for encouragement and thanksgiving. I do not wish to allow the occasion to pass without reference in this house to the successes of the Soviet forces under the leadership of Premier Stalin. The whole free world is in their debt for what they have done to withstand the German invaders and to drive them from many thousands of square miles of Soviet territory. May their arms continue to be successful until victory over our common enemy is achieved.
Speaking of Russia's successes I should like to repeat in this house a warning which Mr. Eden gave to the people of Great Britain in his speech in London on Sunday. The foreign secretary of Great Britain pointed out that German propaganda was trying to succeed where German armies had failed and was making every effort to foster suspicion and encourage dissension between the allies by reviving the bogey of bolshevism and by representing Hitler as the saviour of western civilization. We must be on our guard in Canada against deceptions and propaganda of this kind. Inspired by mutual trust and confidence, begotten of common efforts, let us believe in and work for full and frank cooperation towards victory among all members of the united nations, and after victory has been won, towards a just and durable peace.
The past year has witnessed the establishment of direct diplomatic relations between Canada and the Union of Socialist Soviet Republics, which was announced in this house on June 12. Shortly afterwards we had the pleasure of welcoming to Canada Mr. Feodor Gousev as Soviet minister, and I am glad to be able to inform the house that Mr. Dana Wilgress will shortly establish the first Canadian diplomatic mission in the U.S.S.R. I am sure it is the fervent hope of all Canadians that the establishment of diplomatic relations is but the prelude to a long period of mutual
[Mr. St. Laurpnt.l

Soviet Union
understanding and cooperation between our two peoples, both in the conduct of the war and in the maintenance of a firm and durable
peace.
Impressive figures have recently been made public in the United Kingdom and the United States of the supplies furnished to the Soviet government by the united nations. I should like the people of Canada to know as fully as possible within the limits of military secrecy what portion of these supplies has been produced in Canada.
Out of a total of over six thousand tanks more than one thousand were manufactured in Canada. Two thousand universal carriers have gone forward to the U.S.S.R., as well as quantities of guns and over 22,000,000 rounds of ammunition of various types. We have sent to the Russian people military clothing and supplies. Many shiploads of strategic metals and materials have gone forward from Canada. In the field of foodstuffs the house will recall the Canadian-Soviet credit agreement under which a credit of $10,000,000 was extended to the U.S.S.R. to cover purchases of Canadian wheat and flour. The Canadian people have contributed $1,000,000 to the Canadian Red Cross Society and these funds have been used to supply essential medical supplies vitally needed on the Russian front. The Canadian aid to Russia fund has also completed an appeal for $1,000,000, to which the Canadian public have generously responded by subscribing in cash a sum considerably over $2,000,000. If the value of goods donated were added the total would be considerably over $3,000,000. Thus essential weapons, munitions of war and raw materials, foodstuffs and medical supplies have gone forward from Canada to strengthen the Russian people in the fight, while at the same time Canadian forces, together with their comrades in arms from each of the united nations, have hammered powerful blows against the common enemy.
In paying tribute to the valour and spirit of the Red army our admiration is equalled only by our determination to face the common enemy with like fortitude. To-day our common task in this vast struggle has brought Russia and Canada closer together. To-morrow, when the scourge of fascism has been blasted from the minds of free men everywhere, our peoples must work side by side to aid in the establishment of a world order based on inter-dependence and on the worth of human personality.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: TWENTY-FIFTH ANNIVERSARY OF ESTABLISHMENT OF THE RUSSIAN ARMY-TRIBUTE TO ITS VALOUR AND SPIRIT

Mr. Speaker, I deem it a very great honour and privilege to associate the
TMr. Mackenzie King.]
Progressive Conservative party in this house with what has been said by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). It seems to me particularly appropriate that on this occasion, when the Red army is celebrating its twenty-fifth anniversary, we in Canada should pay a well-deserved tribute to that great ally who in this war has shown a strength which perhaps many of us at one time thought she did not possess. The other day a German propagandist made this statement with respect to the present situation concerning Germany and Russia; that the Russians had broken loose with a power eclipsing all imagination. I think to-day we in Canada are only too pleased to have the opportunity to express something of our feelings and our thoughts with respect to the tenacity, the heroism and the bravery being shown by the Russian people, their army and their government in the interests of freedom and liberty throughout the world. As long as the voice of freedom is heard it will pay tribute to the valour, the endurance and the indomitable pluck of the Red army of Russia in this conflict, and I welcome this opportunity to pay tribute to so honourable and so staunch a fighting ally in this great cause.
Mr. M. J. COLDWELL (Rosetown-Biggar); Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation I too should like to support what has been said by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon). I am sure there is no one in this house or in the country who does not admire the bravery and fortitude with which our Russian allies have withstood the onslaught of a well-prepared, dangerous and bitter foe. A short time ago I was reading Ambassador Davis's "Mission to Moscow", and I was amazed at the appreciation he had, even before Munich, of the strength of the Russian army and the likelihood of its being able to withstand an onslaught from the west. To-day, in endorsing what the Prime Minister has said, may I suggest that it is part of our bounden duty to try to break down the suspicion that still exists in some quarters with regard to Russia, bearing in mind that in the days which will follow this great struggle Russia will play a leading part in the reconstruction of the world. Ever since Russia entered this conflict I have been hopeful that two things might happen: first, that Russia might become rather more democratic in its ways and its methods of government, and second that we, the democratic nations, might become rather more progressive.

I mean "progressive"
in the dictionary meaning of the word; when you tag on to it the word "Conservative" you have a conflict in terms. Therefore I should like to emphasize this hope that the association may do us both good.
I know that in some quarters there still lingers a feeling of fear of a repetition of the bolshevik revolution. Well, revolutions are recorded throughout the pages of history, and apparently the people who brought about those revolutions were not always ashamed of them later. If we look through the pages of our own history we find that in 1649 the English people had a revolution which spilled much blood and chopped off a king's head. The American revolution was a great historic event which also caused a good deal of unnecessary bloodshed, as did the French revolution. But out of these revolutions, deplorable though they were, came something better for the nations involved and something better for mankind; so perhaps, and I think indeed for certain, out of the revolution which took place in Russia we may see something better arise in that country.
May I leave with the house just one further thought. We all applauded when we heard of the splendid manner in which our Canadian people had responded to appeals for aid to Russia. This is as it should be; but I suggest that after all Russia is not asking for charity. I am indeed glad that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), in presenting the resolution concerning the gift to the united nations on behalf of the Canadian people, has included all our allies. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the party with which I am associated I heartily concur in the sentiments expressed by the Prime Minister.

Mr. Speaker, I rise at this earliest opportunity to endeavour to wipe out what amounts to a reflection either intentionally or unintentionally cast upon me in the debate last , night. After I had left the house the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) declared with respect to the nonadoption of the report of the committee on the defence of Canada regulations that it was I who had in effect stood in the way of the report being presented for adoption, and that I was responsible for his, and members of his party, being prevented from securing the adoption of the report. I wish to indicate by the rules of the house how completely inaccurate such a statement or suggestion is. It is true, as I said in the house last night, that there is a measure of responsibility upon me; I freely and frankly took such responsibility last night. The hon. member's remark arose from the fact that I had stated that responsibility for the nonadoption rested on his shoulders as well as on those of other members of his party, and of Other hon. members in the house.
The facts are matters of record. I served notice that I would move the adoption of the report, and after forty-eight hours I was free to do so. But when I did not do so, then according to the rules and practices of the house, as is well known by a number of hon. members in the Cooperative Common-

Privilege-Mr. Maybank
wealth Federation party, any one of them was completely free to move the adoption. I cannot speak with certainty as to whether the hon. member for Cape Breton South was ignorant of or whether he had knowledge upon that particular point. I should have thought he was well aware of the position at all times, and that he himself knew he had that right; but if he would say I am wrong about that, naturally, I would accept his statement. However it is perfectly true that according to the rules and practices of the house it was the right of every hon. member of his party, or of any one of them, to move the adoption of the report, and each of them refrained from doing so.
The house, not I only, was at that time seized of that notice I had given. It was not I only who had the right to move the adoption of the report. It was the right also of the hon. member for Cape Breton South. But if he was not personally aware of his rights, then other hon. members of his party, and in particular his leader, or the hon. member of his group who sat , on the committee, certainly did know the facts. There can be no question about that.
One other point: It was the representative of his party who agreed with others-not with me, because I was not in agreement- that the adoption of the report should not be moved.

speechtext: The house resumed from Friday, February 19, consideration of the motion of Mr. W. E. Harris (Grey-Bruce) for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Graydon, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Cardin.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose on Friday night I had been speaking for about half an hour, and, as I remember, I was setting forth the reasons why my group would oppose the amendment moved by the hon. member for Richelieu-Vereheres (Mr. Cardin). During the course of my remarks I stated why I believed the motion had been made. I thought it was rather a motion of protest on the part of a considerable section of the people of Canada as represented by the hon. member who moved the amendment. I still believe that to be so. At the same time within the amendment itself two reasons are set forth to justify it. As I understand it, the first is that there is confusion throughout the dominion with respect to labour, and the second is that there is a fear that we shall not have the production which is necessary.

I should like to deal with that aspect of the amendment.
We grant that the whole labour situation in Canada is in a muddle, and we believe that every aspect of it should be examined. We contend that the entire state of affairs as regards this matter ought to be clarified and the various inadequacies adjusted. If the government has fallen down in any one thing more than another since the beginning of the .war it has been in the management of the labour supply of the country. The government has been guilty of making grievous mistakes with respect to labour, and within the next few months I feel sure we shall see a clear manifestation of that fact. Then he who runs may read.
We agree that a parliamentary committee ought to be struck, as suggested by the hon. member in his amendment. This committee should investigate objectively and intensively and completely the labour conditions throughout Canada. It seems to me that a number of departments are involved in the labour question. Obviously the three departments which are concerned with the defence of the country are interested; then there is the Department of Labour and the national selective service branch. At various stages other departments have been involved; they seem to be falling over each other and creating confusion, and the result is that hardly anyone knows just what is what with respect to labour. Even the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has had to step in occasionally and give us a speech setting forth what was to happen, and the result is we just do not know what the position is. A committee charged with the responsibility of ascertaining all the facts in regard to the matter would be doing a service to this country, and I agree with the hon. member in that respect.
I believe also that the whole food situation in Canada ought to be canvassed with the greatest care. I have indicated my feeling in this respect before. The fuel situation is far graver than most people realize; there is much danger of a serious and painful fuel shortage next year which may affect people from end to end of this country. This parliament ought to examine into the situation so that we may know just how serious it is and provide the necessary remedies. Housing conditions in Canada should also be examined into; they are partly a result of the labour situation. Then the matter of transportation, referred to in the amendment, should be investigated. It is my belief that there is plenty of man-power and woman-power in Canada provided that it is wisely and effectively mobilized and applied w'here it is needed.

The Address-Mr. Brunelle
One example that comes to mind is the mismanagement of labour with respect to gold. This point has been dealt with already in some measure in this house by certain hon. members. I understand that something like 22,000 men in Canada are still engaged in the useless work of producing gold. I understand also that over S200,000,000 worth of gold is being produced in this country. Of what conceivable value it can be is beyond the power of anyone who faces the facts to decide.
There is another matter in connection with which I think we should have a committee. As I say, I believe" that this amendment is a protest by reason of the feeling which exists between a great many French-Canadian people and English-Canadian people. A committee should be appointed at this session whose work should be to examine into the whole situation that exists between the two great races of Canada. The object of this committee should be the bringing about of conditions that will be fair to both races. I have heard statements made by some of my French-Canadian compatriots to the effect that they feel they are being discriminated against in connection with the economic affairs of this country. That may be so; I am inclined to think that it is so. That matter should be looked into; the truth should be found out and equal treatment given to everybody from one end of Canada to the other. It should be done at this session, before anything serious develops. The committee should consist of representatives of both races, and the representation should be such as to make everyone feel satisfied that justice will be done, that the whole case will be heard. Every province should be adequately represented, as well as every party, so that there can be a non-political, unprejudiced investigation into the whole question. Thus we might create harmony, good feeling and good will between the two great races whom destiny and providence have ordained should work together in the building of Canada.
I believe that these committees would do a great deal of good in the country. To that extent I agree with the hon. member's amendment. However, I do not think the working of the mobilization act should be suspended until the committee has finished its work. The committee could work just as well while the war effort of this country was going forward under the National Resources Mobilization Act. Therefore I am going to oppose the amendment on the ground that the suspension of this act and the disruption of the country's war effort are unnecessary.
There is another matter which should be taken care of in connection with this whole question. Canada should remove at once the

financial restrictions which are hampering the country at every turn and which are creating unpleasant and probably injurious incidents between the French-Canadian and the English-Canadian people. If Canada were to free herself of all financial restrictions and base her war effort and her economy purely on the man-power and material resources which we have, we should find it easier to clear up many of the difficulties which have caused the feeling which has given rise to the subamendment.
We could reward men for going into the various activities into which we wish them to go. Many people of Canada up to the present time have not realized that we could have encouraged men to join the army in such numbers that we would have found it difficult to keep out of the army a sufficient number of men to carry on the rest of the nation's business. As I say, we could reward men for going to war simply by promising them sufficient financial consideration and thus providing that they should be not worse off but better off for enlisting. We could get men to go into agriculture or any other activity by the simple method of rewarding them adequately for so doing. Consequently, if Canada were in control of the financial mechanism which is operative in this country and if she exercised that financial mechanism with the object of mobilizing all our resources, we should overcome much of the ill-feeling which has developed.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after some hesitation I have decided to say a few words on the amendment of the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin). In a pressing appeal for support of this amendment the hon. member for Temis-couata (Mr. Pouliot) the other day made references to some of the members who spoke in the debate on the address and discussed man-power and the labour shortage on the farms. I was one of the members who spoke in the debate on the address and touched on those questions, but surely not in the way that the hon. member for Temiscouata implied. Indeed I think I did the very opposite. I did not criticize the government any more than the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) or the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) criticized the government. I said that the Conservative party, having advocated for over three and a half years the conscription of more and more men, were now complaining that there was a shortage of men on the farms, and I congratulated the government upon having followed the policy of a balanced war effort. I also stressed the
The Address-Mr. Brunelle

importance of agriculture and the necessity of its being continued unimpaired. I quoted some authorities in support of my contention and ended by saying that the welfare of the farmers, while in the hands of the Minister of Agriculture was well safeguarded.
I could reply to some other urgings and coaxings and pleadings which have been made recently and which are based on predictions and prophecies, but in order to save time I shall not do so. I repeat to-day what I said the other day, and I am consistent, I believe, in voting against the amendment of the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres, as I intend to do. Far be it from me to lecture anybody, but I think that in matters which are open to controversy it is often expedient to let well enough alone, particularly in this case, knowing the circumstances under which the mobilization law was passed and knowing the manner and extent of its application. In all these circumstances the act offers a singularly good occasion for letting well enough alone. I shall say no more on that, and I am sure I shall be understood.
This session, Mr. Speaker, has just begun. The members have come here to report on what has taken place in their respective constituencies since the adjournment of the house last fall. The members have already done that duty and have reported to the government what they have found. They have pointed out that great care must be taken in enlisting more men because enlistments seem to have reached what I might term the saturation point. More than ever do I think that the speech from the throne this year has afforded us an opportunity for a debate which has been very useful. We have been able to talk upon any subject. The members have come here from their constituencies with very recent knowledge of what their constituents have told them, and in turn they have been able to tell the government what is taking place throughout the country. The ministers, who are all shrewd men, have listened, and I submit that they have already begun to remedy the present situation. For instance, the Minister of Agriculture in his address in this house on February 9, put on Hansard a letter which has already been addressed to all directors of boards in charge of granting exemptions or postponements of military service. 1 beg leave to quote only two or three paragraphs of this letter:
This is the first of such letters which will be issued by the labour department.
This means that other letters will be sent and that further steps may be taken to remedy the situation. I quote further:

The growing scarcity of agricultural labour makes it increasingly important that essential agricultural workers be encouraged to remain on farms.
Further:
Farm workers who apply for postponement of military training are to be granted postponement until further notice.
This good beginning is sufficient to make me trust the government and believe that whenever the occasion arises other remedies will be applied. In any event, Mr. Speaker, I believe that any investigation which may be made into the shortage of man-power on the farm should be conducted by the ministers themselves. It is their responsibility. I have complained, as almost every other member of the house has done, of the fact- and the fact is an inevitable one-that too much of the responsibility of the ministers is being transferred to somebody else. My friend the member for Richelieu-Vercheres, whom I esteem very much, has himself complained that too many boards and commissions were made to assume the responsibilities of the ministers, I like to approve and follow the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres whenever he is right, and I think he was right when he said that. But in moving the amendment which is now before the house I do not think he agrees with what he said in the speech he made on the address only a few days ago, and I am sorry I cannot follow him this time.
The organization of our immense national resources was a tremendous job. It has been done well by our ministers; and happily this country had at its head the best brains and the most brilliant administrative minds that it could have. In saying this I wish to compliment the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres, because he himself was one of the ministers when this mobilization law was framed and passed, and even during the first two years of its operation. In changing the complete national organization from a peacetime to a war-time production it is inevitable that mistakes, will occur, that there will be shortcomings or deficiencies. The shortage of men at the present time is one of those inevitable defects, and I believe the government in charge of the affairs of the country will correct it in due course. When that famous and glorious "new order" is being established the same thing will occur; there will be defects; there will be shortcomings, -but with good will and understanding everyone will do his best to correct those deficiencies and defects. So that to-day, with good will and understanding, the shortage of men on the farms will easily be remedied.
I think that the first duty of hon. members when they came to attend this present session

The Address-Mr. Coldwell
was to make representations to the government and show where remedies should be applied. This we have done. The second duty of members was to afford the government a reasonable opportunity of putting remedial measures into effect. This, I hope, we shall do.
The amendment of the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres means the overthrow of the government; it cannot mean anything else. If my memory serves me rightly, I took this definite and precious opinion from the lips of the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres himself when last year a similar amendment was made to the speech from the throne while he was a minister of the crown. I cannot support such a drastic measure at this time. In spite of the grievances I have-and at a time like this almost everybody has grievances-I retain my faith in the government; and particularly I trust the Prime Minister, whose record as a brilliant administrator and a wise leader of men is the pride of almost every Canadian citizen. I wish to add that as a rule I revolt against the mere idea of following anyone sheepishly or blindly against the dictates of my conscience or the conclusions of my humble judgment. But when I find a really superior man who is honest, who is highly experienced in a matter which happens to concern me, I do not hesitate; I take pride in following him. And to-day the Prime Minister is really a superman. I wish to add, in case somebody may say that I have changed, that last year the situation was quite different. I, in common with other hon. members, had a special and specific mandate to fulfil. This year I am free to act and to vote according to my humble judgment.

Before the amendment to the amendment is voted upon I should like to say a few words, since I was unable to be present on Friday afternoon when the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) placed the considered point of view of our group before the house. As he said then, we shall vote against the amendment to the amendment. We believe that in the midst of this great struggle, when in a very real sense we are fighting for our survival, we could not possibly suspend the operation of any acts or regulations which relate to the conduct of the war. No matter how much we may disapprove policies adopted by the government and subsequently approved by parliament, we hold the view, and I
The Address

Mr. Coldwell

believe it is the proper and! democratic view, that when parliament has given its approval to a certain line of policy it is the duty of members of parliament to support that policy until there is an opportunity of changing it. In peace time one can rise in the House of Commons or elsewhere almost as soon as a policy has been adopted and urge that it be changed; but once we are committed to our allies to taking a certain part in that war, and the war itself is in progress, we must support the policy accepted by parliament under which it is being conducted. That is our position.
I thoroughly agree with my friend the hon. member for Weyburn and others in this house when they point out that the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin) is moved by one who was a member of the government when the policies which we are now discussing were instituted. Therefore there can be little doubt that at that time the hon. member gave his support to them.
Since the war began we in this group have urged on many occasions, beginning with the day the war broke out, that the first thing that should have been done was the making of a thorough survey of all our resources in order to determine in what manner we could best serve the common cause. We believed and stated that if we allowed ourselves to be stampeded in any one direction we might ultimately find ourselves in difficulty as a nation. Ever since this war began there have been those who failed to recognize that this is not a war in which large bodies of men move from place to place or are entrenched, as in former wars, but a mechanized war in which many machines are used, the operators of which not only have to be very highly trained but also have to be supported by large numbers of men in industry and agriculture whose business it is to produce the machines and food required for the conduct of the war. Hence our failure to conceive an over-all plan is very largely the difficulty which we face at the present time.
Our friends to my immediate right have been very interesting to many of us in the house this year. In the first two years of the war we heard from them continuous criticisms to the effect that we were not placing enough men under arms, that we were not preparing to send more and more men into the battle line. This year they have been in agreement with the contention of many other hon. members of the house that in order to maintain those men in the battle line we must have large numbers of well-trained men in our factories and on the farms

producing the commodities required to enable us to play our part in the conduct of this war as we are best able to do.
I am in agreement with the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) who said a few minutes ago that even at this time a useful purpose would be served by accepting at least one of the suggestions made in the proposed subamendment, namely, that a thorough survey even at this late day should be made of our man-power in order to see how best we can apportion it in the several fields of endeavour connected with the war. This must be done not at a time when we are withholding the mobilization of manpower, but when we are actually continuing our mobilization. There is no reason in the world why a thorough survey should not be made and an understanding arrived at of the possibilities of our country. So I say that the suggestion in the subamendment to the effect that a committee be set up to inquire into the man-power problem in this country is a constructive suggestion. But while we regard it as such we could not possibly support an amendment which would withhold from the government at this critical time the right to continue to call men for service in the armed forces.
The problem is not only one of men in the armed forces. As has been properly pointed out by many hon. members in this debate, we require to produce this year larger quantities of food than ever. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) made this very clear to us when he spoke in the present debate. If we are to have the quantity of food produced in this country that is required not only by our own and allied armies but also to assist in feeding people in Europe when the second front is opened in the west and the nations are liberated, then we require to pay particular attention to the problem of man-power on the farm. I noticed that on February 9 the Canadian federation of agriculture placed before the Prime Minister a brief on the subject of man-power in agriculture in which they made the position clear. The spokesmen for the federation stated that it will be impossible to meet the greatly increased production goals if a heavy-drain on the skilled man-power of the farms continues. They went on to say that it was their considered opinion that the increasing shortage in farm labour cannot be met by the unpaid labour of the farmer's wife and young children, nor can skilled labour so essential to present-day farming be replaced by untrained help from the cities, without a decline in the production of food. The federa-

The Address-Mr. Tremblay
tion recommended that to ensure an adequate supply of skilled farm help the allocation of the available man-power supply should be made without discrimination between agriculture and other essential war industries. For peak labour demands during seeding and harvest, they suggest that military authorities should release men in /military training and that the steps necessary to this end should be taken in ample time to meet the situation. These were constructive proposals from the federation of agriculture which I would warmly commend to the minister.
Underlining the man-power muddle in which we find ourselves, a return for which I asked before the house met, which was tabled on February 10, indicates clearly how serious the situation is, not only because we have shortages in some fields of vital industry but also because we have at the present time a great deal of unemployment.
I asked for a return indicating the number of persons registered as seeking work at the regional employment offices, five in number. I find, for example, that on January 14 of this year there were 96,331 persons so registered, and I believe that number has since risen to some extent. This emphasizes the plea that we should have some investigation into our man-power policy in order that we may serve to the greatest extent possible the needs of this country and of the war effort. The group with -which I am associated has continually urged that an all-out war effort requires not only the mobilization and organization of our human resources but, even more fundamentally, the organization on the same terms and the same basis of industry and wealth. If we are going to have an all-out war effort, we must do exactly that.
Before I sit down there is just one other thing I should like to say. I hope during this session of parliament we may be able to end the kind of controversy about the war effort that from time to time we have had to endure here. If we could only realize that to-day we are in very truth fighting a war of survival; that while we may hold different views and advocate different policies it should be the duty of all to endeavour to see to it that the war effort of our country is a maximum contribution to the common cause of defeating the aggressor powers. So that while it seems to me the time is long past when we should have formulated a thorough-going, comprehensive, over-all war plan for this country, at least now that time ought to be here in a very real sense. As I say, we should endeavour during this session to see to it that we make our maximum effort in the conduct of the war and that the man-power, financial and 72537-41
economic resources of the country are utilized to the very best effect. This cannot be done by overemphasizing one phase or the other of our national effort. We should endeavour to see each part of our great effort in its own true and proper perspective. Only in that way can we make our maximum contribution to the common cause.

Mr. Speaker, I have no wish to conceal the fact that I feel reluctant to rise at this time in order to voice views at variance with those suggested by the amendment moved by the honourable member for Riche-lieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin). If I find it so painful to contradict him it is because for so many years-and for my part I might say since my early youth-we had been used to see the mover of the amendment at the head of the Liberal forces in our good old province of Quebec, and we were fond of hearing the redoubtable fighter endowed with such captivating and convincing eloquence. We enjoyed following him when he campaigned in company with the late lamented Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe and indeed we had every reason to admire and esteem him. If most of us cannot follow him to-day he may nevertheless be sure that he still enjoys our full esteem. Of course we are sorry that he has seen fit to leave the government which has and will continue to have our unflinching support.
I may say about his amendment that it expresses some of our feelings. Thus when the hon. member states:
"This house is of the opinion that in view of the recognized shortage of farm labour, also the admitted shortage of labour in war industries and in other essential industrial and transportation activities, . . .
When he voices such a regret, I can tell him that most of us fully agree with him. I, for one, have had an opportunity of representing to the proper authorities that they should make available to farmers such help as is essential to the production required for our armed forces and for our allies.
In Quebec military district No. 5, the responsible authorities-or what we call the deferment board-have as a rule granted postponements to those who could prove that they were bona fide farmers. Unfortunately, our young farmers, not very conversant with the law, have often failed to answer the first call and to apply for the postponement to which they were entitled. On the other hand the deferment board was rather inclined to follow the letter rather than observe the spirit of the law, and in this, as in everything, the letter killeth while the spirit giveth life.

The Address-Mr. Tremblay

So that quite recently, on February 3. to be exact, the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) sent a letter to the chairman of the mobilization boards-that is to the postponement boards-containing instructions and an interpretation of the mobilization act. I think it important that certain parts of this letter be put on Hansard so that our farmers might be made aware of the privileges to which they are entitled and which should be granted them when they apply to the mobilization board for a postponement. This letter is dated February 3 and reads in part as follows:
It is the intention of the regulations that agricultural workers are to be retained in agricultural employment as far as practical through the national selective service (civilian) regulations. To the extent that their services can he spared from the farms during the "off-crop" season they are to be encouraged to take temporary seasonal employment in lumbering and logging, forestry, fishing, coal and base metal mining, and acceptance of seasonal work in such industries does not deprive men of their right to postponement as agricultural workers providing they return to farm work when the season re-opens.
I have often been asked, I might say, practically every day by visitors who come to see me and by electors who tell me: I have been granted a postponement, and I would like to know if I am permitted to work in the bush this winter, or to work elsewhere during the "off-season", so as to earn a few extra dollars. Well, farmers should be better informed of the interpretation of the law as given in this letter and be in a position to take advantage of this privilege. It should be made very clear to them, and on this subject the minister not only stated that they have this right, but that they should be encouraged to take advantage of it.
I also wished to call the attention of the house to this letter because the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres, on Friday last, stated that he was sorry that the farm worker was not left on the farm where he was so badly needed. Now this letter shows clearly that even before this statement was made, the Minister of Labour had sent instructions to the chairman of the mobilization boards telling them to leave the farm workers on the farms where they are needed.
In paragraph 4 of this letter, the minister states:
Farm workers who apply for postponement of military training are to be granted postponement until further notice.
I must admit that a more favourable explanation is given here of the mobilization policy of the government. Ever since this act came into force our good farmers did not know where to apply. They had to fill in

forms which, as we all know, even professional men can hardly understand. Then they had to get letters from their mayor, their parish priest, or from some distinguished or other responsible person and prove that they were farmers. Their cases had to be proved beyond all doubt or else their application was immediately turned down. I wish here to call the attention of the government on this fact- unfortunately we have in the army to-day farmers that are needed on the farm and who came up for military service for lack of information concerning the procedure to be followed to obtain postponement. I hope the government will consider this situation and make sure that it is remedied.
Paragraph 4 states that:
Farm workers who apply for postponement from military training are to be granted postponement until further notice, unless it is established that the applicant is not an essential worker in agriculture. It should be noted that the regulations do not require the farmer to produce proof that he is an essential farm worker. If the board doubts that a man is an essential farm worker, even though postponement until further notice is given, it can always exercise the right to deny postponement by calling such a man before the board when established facts are presented.
This is my understanding of the matter- and I would ask the hon. minister to correct me if I am mistaken; a farmer or a farm hand is not obliged to prove that he belongs to that particular class. If the board is of the opinion that he is not a farmer, it is up to the board to prove it. Yesterday, upon meeting the Minister of Labour, I submitted precisely such an interpretation and the minister assured me it was absolutely what the Department of Labour wished to see put into force.
Now then; I now quote paragraph 5 of the letter:
If a worker who upon receipt of "order- medical examination" claims to be an agricultural worker but is not considered by the board to be essential to the operation of a specific farm-the question then arises as to whether or not he is essential to agriculture in the district.
If agricultural labour is needed in the district, he should be given an opportunity to place himself in a position where his services would be essential to agriculture on some other farm; or in the alternative to increase the production of a specific farm. The board could give a deferment for three months instead of "granting postponement until further notice" in order to give the man an opportunity of finding essential work.
Here again, an improvement is evident. Let us take, for example, the case of a farmer who has three sons at home and only needs two absolutely to run the farm and does not need the third who consequently is

The Address-Mr. Picard
not an essential worker, the board must grant a postponement of three months to the latter thus giving him an opportunity to find employment on some other farm in his district where his services will be required and essential to agriculture. The board, moreover, must grant him an exemption for the time during which he will do some essential work on another farm. It is one of two things: either the government are sincere ar they are not. The government is sincere, of that I am convinced; they want the farmer to produce and to produce as much as he can. Hence the new interpretation given to the mobilization act. I therefore congratulate the government and particularly the Minister of Labour on the instructions issued to competent authorities, and I now hope that the government will see to it that this interpretation is accepted by the mobilization boards throughout Canada.
The hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres to-day, after deploring the conditions which the government must remedy, urges us to give a vote which would express a want of confidence in the government.
His own statement, however, according to the Citizen of February 22, is as follows:
Hon. Mr. Cardin said in an interview here Saturday it was not his intention through his subamendment introduced Thursday in the throne speech debate to force the formation of a national government or to consolidate groups of Quebec members opposed to the government's man power policy.
The honourable member was stating, no doubt, his honest opinion. He himself has told us on a previous occasion-and we believed him-that any government other than that of the present Right Honourable Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) would offer no guarantee that the province of Quebec and its feelings would be respected as they are by the present Prime Minister. I do not believe it was the honourable member's intention to precipitate a want of confidence motion against the King administration. He himself has said as much. However, he states further:
Mr. Cardin admitted his subamendment could be interpreted as a want of confidence motion but "essentially it was not intended as such."
A little further on the article continues:
However, Mr. Cardin was "perfectly sure" the government would not suffer a defeat on his subamendment.
From this, it might be deduced that the hon. member, while intending to blame the government, does not wish to be unfair. I hope that he desires the conversion rather than the death of the sinner, if there is a
sinner. Just the same, it may be inferred from his statements that he does not wish the fall of the present administration. But in what position do we find ourselves? The adoption of this amendment would constitute a censure of the government, expressed by a vote of want of confidence from the hon. members. By voting for the amendment, we would express a wish to overthrow the government and we do overthrow them technically as well as practically.
I may say that popular sentiment in the province of Quebec favours our support of the government who alone offer a guarantee that our legitimate requests as well as our rights will be respected. The hon. Prime Minister surely enjoys not only the confidence of the great majority of my fellow-citizens, but even the esteem and affection of nearly 100 per cent of the population. During the 1940 election, especially in my constituency, there have been, for a certain time, dissatisfied people. One of them, known as a Liberal, not a very fervent or steadfast one, even ran against me. In Dorchester, even among the leaders and the rank and file of Conservatives who gave me their support, it was stated: "We want Tremblay because we know that he will not detach himself from Mackenzie King in the House of Commons." Which goes far to show the sincerity of my stand. I have always taken this attitude with my constituents, with those of other constituencies, of the entire province and1 even of other provinces, when I have supported candidates outside Quebec who were standing for election. My attitude to-day has not changed. I have faith in the hon. leader of the present government; I have faith in his ministers and my vote against the amendment moved by the hon. member, will express this confidence.

Mr. Speaker, the universe is ablaze; for the last three and a half years the world has been ravaged by one of the worst wars that has ever come upon humanity in all history. Two groups of nations are facing each other; two ideologies are trying to destroy one another. Three and a half years ago Canada made its choice and sided with the democracies. When the proposal to declare war was brought before this house few members raised their voice against it; it was carried without a recorded vote. Since that time Canada has made a splendid effort under the present government. Our industrial machine has been geared to produce more than we ever thought it could. Our agricultural production has been raised to new levels. A strong army is now under
The Address-Mr. Picard

arms and our navy has been multiplied more than five times. We have more than 150,000 men in the air force and have contributed more than any other nation in the commonwealth to this splendid plan which has provided airmen for the united nations. All this has been done by progressive steps, with the least disturbance of the normal life of the country and the preservation of national unity; it has been done under the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King).
In considering the present amendment to the amendment every hon. member should ask himself what his attitude was in the past, what it has been up to now and what will be the logical attitude to take on it. In 1940 a vast majority of the members from Quebec supported the bill to provide for the mobilization of the human and national resources of the country. During the following three and a half years if the members from Quebec have been at variance with the government to any great extent, it was on Bill No. 80. French Canadians want to win the war and they want to win it under the present government.
If I may be permitted to talk about my own views and ideas I would say that in the past I have been against our fighting the wars of the British empire unless Canada was directly concerned. My views have not changed. But this is not a war being waged for the pleasure or the aggrandizement of the British empire; this is a world war, a war in which our own institutions are at stake. Canada, whether it is French or English, whether it is the east or the west, stands united on this question. While we may differ as to the best methods to be used to achieve the desired result, we are all convinced that Canada has a better chance to achieve this without disrupting national unity under the leadership of the present Prime Minister.
French Canada has accepted the mobilization of our youth for the defence of Canada and it has volunteered in much larger numbers than it did under the different methods used during the last war. The law that now governs this mobilization was voted upon by a great majority of the members from Quebec. That law is still the same, and that is the law that this amendment to the amendment would suspend. Men will be needed on the other side and volunteers will be taken out of the ranks of many of the regiments now defending our country. Men will be needed to train for the defence of Canada. Nothing has been changed. The law was passed with that intention and despite Bill No. 80 it is still being operated in that spirit.
Under Bill No. 80 the government is given the power to send men overseas, but I do not
(Mr. Picard.]
think that power has ben exercised except to send men to Labrador, Newfoundland and Alaska. I may say that I have had the approval of meetings in my district where I have been told that they have no objection to men being used for the defence of the hemisphere in Labrador or elsewhere, but they are against our men being used on the other continent. This attitude has been approved by French Canada at large, and I am sure that many other hon. members from Quebec will say the same thing. Nothing has been changed and the government is still tied to the declaration that whenever it passed the order in council to use conscripts for overseas service, it would bring it before the house for approval or disapproval on a confidence motion. So that the members from Quebec are still just as free as they were before to vote confidence in the government now; they are in the same position as they were when they voted for the mobilization act in 1940.
What I stated in my speech a few days ago in the debate on the address I still repeat. My good friend the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) reminded the house the other day that I was one of those who had talked about man-power and criticized the government's policy. What I criticized was the operation and the interpretation by the boards of the mobilization regulations, and I still say that clearer instructions should be given to all these boards dealing with deferments or exemptions of farmers or workers in industry. I still think those instructions should be made clearer, but that is a question of interpretation and a question of the operation of the lawv It is not a question of principle as to whether the government has taken the right course in carrying out the mobilization act. It is just a question of knowing whether the government has instructed the boards as to the proper interpretation of the rules, and whether the boards interpret them in such a way as to ensure a proper flow of workers for the farms and for industry. Should we now suspend that law and say to the rest of the world: We will deliberate for months to find out if we have enough men at work or not in industries and agriculture? Should we say at a time like this: Let us wait-German armies may be on the march here and there, and it is true we want to win the war, but let us Wait and argue before committees for months in order to please a certain element of the electorate? I would rather be defeated, Mr. Speaker, than support such a proposal. The whole world would gape in astonishment if they saw any democratic institution in one of the united nations waiting and arguing for months as to whether we have enough men on the farm or

The Address-Mr. Picard
otherwise. I have enough confidence in the government to believe that if abuses have crept into the administration of the law on account of a misinterpretation of the rules, and the facts are brought to their attention, they will be clever enough to correct those abuses. May I say with all due respect to the house that the people have more confidence in the Prime Minister himself settling this question than they would have even in a committee of this house.
People have evoked in the last two years quite frequently the name of a man whose memory is so dear to me that I feel I should say a word about him to-day. The hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin) mentioned his name in the house the other day, and if there is any who has the right to do it, it. is the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres. For him I have the greatest respect, because he has rendered great service to the country, and no matter what people in other parts of the country may think of his present amendment they should bow to him because in moments of crisis in the past he knew what to do. He stood where he should, and he used his great influence at the time with the people of his province to get them in the right way. He deserves the gratitude of the people of this country for his past services, but on this question we cannot follow him.
I have as much right as any to evoke the memory of Lapointe, whether here or in public gatherings. I knew Mr. Lapointe for some thirty years, ever since I was a child. I knew him as his secretary for twelve years, and without boasting I think I may say I enjoyed some of his confidence. Frankly, those who tried to picture Mr. Lapointe, as some have tried at meetings of the Defence of Canada League, are either not sincere or they know very little of the man. There is one thing that Lapointe had, and that was a true sentiment for Canada at large, not only for his province but for the whole country. He was one hundred per cent a Canadian. Lapointe was a disciple of Laurier, and he believed in the true Liberalism of Laurier. He went further and believed in the true Liberalism of the English school of Gladstone and so many other leaders on the other side. He was, above all, for a united Canada. He would not have given one inch of ground on matters of interest to his compatriots where a question of principle was concerned. But in matters where the interests of the whole country were concerned he would have thought as a Canadian above all else.
Lapointe at any moment was ready to fight bigotry where he found it and when he thought that it would hurt Canada. In English Canada
he would fight men like Shields and others who are trying every day to stir up racial hatred. In his own province he preached a better understanding and fought all his life against the extremists from the days of 1910 when he fought nationalism, and successfully in his own constituency; when he stood by Laurier on the question of the navy. When people said that Kamouraslca would turn against him, Lapointe summoned a meeting of his people the day after he returned to his constituency from Ottawa and got his people to follow him. He was not one of those to flinch. The people stood behind him and he was sent back to Ottawa. It was those who had hesitated to follow Laurier who were defeated at the next election by Nationalists, and not those who had remained steadfast. Lapointe in Quebec in his last years had enough trouble fighting the views and sentiments preached by the Bouchards and other separatists who came against him, sometimes with the silent support of the official opposition. Everybody will remember Lapointe's attitude during this war, and none of those who vote against this amendment should think that he is not in the true line with Lapointe. That was true also, at the time, of the member for Richelieu-Vercheres. He then stood by Lapointe and the two deserved credit. I again pay my due respect to the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres, whose true Liberalism for a quarter of a centuiy has been an example for all of us, whose views I cannot share now, but whose sincerity I would not question. But I cannot follow him in the steps he is now taking. The hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres sat here on Laurier's side; he was one of his disciples. Does he think for one moment that Laurier would bring in such an amendment as this? If he does, I respectfully differ; I do not think so.
Mr. Lapointe before his death said on many occasions that he had not changed his attitude as to Canada's participation in this war to the utmost, with this reservation, which he had given to his friends and compatriots, that he would not ask them to be conscripted for the defence of Canada overseas. But he said he would support everything short of that to win the war, and if he ever came to the conclusion that that was necessaiy, he would withdraw himself rather than do it, because of the undertaking he had given.
That was the attitude of Lapointe. I say, if Lapointe were living he would be sad, even sadder than we are, to see this house faced with such an amendment to the amendment. Lapointe, had he lived, would not have brought forward such a subamendment; and
The Address-Mr. Lajontaine

I can assure you, sir, that the vast majority of the members from his province will be true to him, and will vote against it.
