speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I rise at this stage of the debate to speak on the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin), it is because of the fact that I want to give to this house and place on Hansard the reasons which, I think, will justify my voting the way I intend to vote when the division is called.
During the 1940 election, I visited all the parishes of the constituency of Megantic-Frontenac which I have the honour to represent in this house. Addressing all the electors of those parishes, I then stated sincerely and frankly what, if I were elected, my attitude would be on any questions which might arise, such as the very question which is now before the house.
At those meetings, in the light of statements made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), the late lamented Ernest Lapointe and the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin) who was then Minister of Public Works, I pledged myself to do two things.
First, I promised to oppose any measure or bill of conscription for overseas service; second, I promised to oppose any union or coalition government, a dream so dearly cherished by a number of members sitting on the opposite side of the house. These are the only two specific promises I have made to my electors and I may state, Mr. Speaker, that I will keep them at all cost, being convinced that keeping my word is preferable to any honours that might be conferred on me.
Moreover, at each of the meetings at which I made those promises, I declared that, in view of the war we were waging at the side of France and England, I could foresee dark and difficult days ahead. I stated that we might be faced with complex problems, such as those that confronted us during the last session and such as the present one, but that, realizing the extent of my responsibility, I would consider all these questions in the light of circumstances and in relation to the facts and arguments expounded and that I would vote according to the dictates of my conscience. I have been faithful to this policy ever since I came to this house and I will adhere to it when the time comes to vote on the motion before the house.
What does the amendment moved by the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin) refer to? It appears at page 551 of Hansard, as follows:

This house is of the opinion that in view of the recognized shortage of farm labour, also the admitted shortage of labour in war industries and in other essential industrial and transportation activities, Your Excellency's advisers should have provided for the withholding of the operation of the National Resources Mobilization Act in regard to the raising of men for military service until, at least, a complete investigation is made by a committee of the house, to ascertain and determine by what means or methods Canada can now most effectively contribute to the winning of the war, without destroying the economic, social and national life of the country.
Scarcity of farm labour. No doubt remains in the minds of anyone regarding the scarcity of farm labour; but should this scarcity be blamed on the mobilization act exclusively? I do not think so, for you know that the regulations enacted under this act permit farmers' sons and farm workers to obtain a postponement of training until a specified date or until further notice.
Any man, whether a farmer, a farmer's son or a farm worker, when notified to report for his medical examination could, within eight days of the receipt of such notice, apply for postponement or extension by duly completing the questionnaire enclosed with the notice and returning it to the registrar of his division. The latter would submit the case to the board set up for the purpose, which passed upon the advisability of granting or declining suspension or postponement of the call-up in the light of the reasons set forth in the application.
May I be allowed to mention incidentally, Mr. Speaker, that all men in Division F who were called up under this Act have been treated with fairness and impartiality, both by the registrar and his staff, who invariably made it their duty to supply all the information requested by those r jncerned, and by the members of the board In so far as I know-and I am conversant with the question-they have discharged their duties in a fair and sensible manner. There may have been and, undoubtedly, there were some mistakes made, but they were made unintentionally and, in most cases they were due to a lack of knowledge or a lack of attention on the part of the applicant in filling the application for postponement. In every case where an applicant deserved a postponement, such postponement was granted. If, as I have just stated, all true farmers, their sons and their employees were granted a' delay or a postponement until further notice, as has been the case in Division F, then the Mobilization Act cannot be held responsible for the present scarcity of farm labour. I am inclined to believe, on the contrary, that it was caused by the large number of farmers who, lured by the industrial

The Address-Mr. Fauteux
areas, their war munition and equipment industries and the high wages paid, have forsaken the farm for the cities. Of this, Sorel, the home town of the hon. member for Riehelieu-Vercheres offers a typical example; its population has nearly doubled since 1939 on account of its war industries.
The same condition obtains in the city of Quebec whose population has considerably increased during the past two years. The amendment says:
Until, at least, a complete investigation is made by a committee of the house to ascertain and determine by what means or methods Canada can now most effectively contribute to the winning of the war.
I oppose the setting up of such a committee, for I feel that a measure of this sort might be a step toward the establishment of a union government. Anybody familiar with the setting up of a committee of the house is aware that such a committee is made up of members belonging to every party. Is it not exactly in this fashion that the union government of 1917 was organized? The amendment continues:
Without destroying the economic, social and national life of the country.
I am wondering, at least up to the present moment, where is to be found the (lost ruction of the economic life of the country and how it could be destroyed, even though the industries of war require more workers.
Just now, more people are at work than at any other time in our history; the salaries are just as high, or perhaps higher, than they have ever been.
To support what I have just said, may I be permitted to sketch the part played by war industry in Quebec? As regards implements of war, four of the nine types of aircraft made in Canada are manufactured in the province of Quebec. The largest plant in the British Empire manufacturing 25-pounders, from the raw materials to the finished products, is located in the province of Quebec. Our province manufactures and assembles two types of tanks, and turns out every kind of aerial bombs. It has two of the largest shell factories and half a dozen shipyards which launch cargo-boats, corvettes and minesweepers. Sixty per cent of the Canadian soldiers walk in shoes made in our province, which turns out, in large quantities, parachutes, bullets, cartridges, trench mortars, chemical products, explosives, and electrical and wireless apparatus.
The aluminum industry has built there one of the largest plants in the world. The province of Quebec is the centre of the newsprint industry. Pulp and paper, essential products
in modern warfare, are manufactured in our province, and the capital invested in that industry amounts to $360,000,000. Our province produces more rayon than any other province. As to the mining industry, we can say that the fabulous resources of our province saved the allies from a difficult situation. Aluminum, copper, asbestos are our main products, but other strategical products badly needed by the united nations, such as manganese, tungsten, molybdenum and chromium, are to be found in our province and are in process of development.
The weekly earnings of the 600,000 industrial workers of Quebec amount to $16,300,000. They produce the whole of Canadian aluminum; they operate one of the largest tank factories on the continent; they produce planes and ships in vast numbers.
In view of such facts and figures, I do not believe that the government have been, nor are they now, leading us toward economic ruin; quite the contrary, they have given us a kind of prosperity.
Whatever may be said to disprove it, the amendment as drafted, were it adopted by the house, would constitute a non-confidence vote against the government. As there is nothing in the speech from the throne which is contrary to the obligations I have taken toward my constituents, I shall vote against this amendment and I shall support the government, for I have every confidence in them.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not without a feeling of emotion and without fvdly realizing my responsibilities that I rise to address the house. Since the hon. member for Riehelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin) has moved the amendment which is familiar to all of us, I believe we can truthfully say that the province of Quebec has been deeply stirred. One cannot rise in this house and speak for or against that amendment without first realizing that he shall have to speak for or against the mover, the hon. member for Riehelieu-Vercheres, the former minister of public works.
The hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) stated the other day that during the thirty-odd years of his political life, he had perhaps never witnessed such a momentous occasion. I am not much advanced in years, Mr. Speaker, but still I have been in politics for about twenty years. I come from a family which is active in politics and which has taken a part in the development of our province, and if I rise in this house to-day, I may say, with all due deference to my good friend the hon. member for Temiscouata, that
The Address-Mr. Fautewx

it is not for the sake of the Christmas tree or the gifts that may hang on it. But, before registering my vote I simply wish to explain my stand. And, as I said at the outset, it is exceedingly difficulty for a member from the province of Quebec to speak on the amendment. The hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres must certainly be aware that the whole province and all the members, even those who do not see eye to eye with him and who will vote against his motion, have nevertheless much affection and admiration for him.
However, the electors of our respective constituencies have sent us here not from any considerations of friendship or affection, but to fulfil our duty, all our duty. And if we must not vote for the gift hanging from the Christmas tree, neither must we be prompted to vote by any fear of the pack of any organization, or of a press which I dare not style as I should, and which is striving neither for national unity in Canada, nor for the greater good of Quebec, not for the defence of Canada, but for a single cause, which is to assume power both in Quebec and in Ottawa.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres will permit me, I shall quote a few remarks of his which still move me deeply and which, if they were true and heartfelt when he made them over the radio, must still hold true in this debate.
On April 24, 1942, the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres, speaking over the radio on the question of the plebiscite, made a marvellous speech that we all like to remember. At the beginning of his speech, he said:
The discussion of the great problem of to-day has upset and worried the minds of many people, especially amongst the French-speaking population of this province. I am old enough to remember a similar campaign that was made in 1911, the year I entered politics. Laurier was then thrown out of power following the attacks hurled against him by his compatriots of the province of Quebec. The men and women of my age remember it as they remember also the consequences of that serious blunder.
The famous navy question was then to the fore. In certain parts of the country, Laurier was accused of not being imperialistic enough. . . .
The same thing is said to-day about Mr. King.
. . . and his idea of establishing a Canadian navy was laughed at; and in the province of Quebec, he was accused of having sold his country to England. . . .
History repeats itself, Mr. Speaker.
. . . and it appeared that the campaign in the province of Quebec was financed from outside, by Mr. Borden's supporters, through the imperialistic fund. These people were then trying to divide the province of Quebec so as to succeed in throwing Laurier out of power. How many false declarations of independence did we not [Mr. Fauteux.l
hear then, how many self-seeking denunciations against so-called political partisanship. . . .
We are called "yes-men" today
. . . accusations of weakness and treachery, in short, appeals to prejudice. It was very much like what we hear to-day, save that the leaders of the movement at the time were more important and more gifted.
A few of the would-be saviours of that time can still be found to-day taking part in this agitation. They are somewhat older, but appear not to have learned from experience, probably because they have not personally suffered from the conditions which they contributed to bring about. These agitators claimed that Laurier was a coward and a traitor, that he was bent on retaining power at any price and that he had sold out to England.
It was then possible to frighten the people of Quebec and many honest individuals were taken in for lack of a proper understanding of actual facts and of the grave situation of the moment. As a result, under attacks coming from two opposite directions, but supported, it has been said, by funds coming from the same source, Laurier was overthrown. Sir Robert Borden succeeded him at the head of affairs and it was under his leadership that we had the would-be union government of 1917. Those who had remained faithful to Laurier stood with him in the opposition. They still could protest, but having lost power, they were forced to submit to the law as imposed by the majority,
I call upon my province and my colleagues not to forget that statement. Therein lies perhaps my motive for rising in my seat to-day, Mr. Speaker. In 1911, I had not, like the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres, the privilege of waging the political campaign at the side of Laurier. I was then but a boy at the Quebec seminary. But I perfectly recall how Laurier, our leader, defeated candidate in Quebec East, the man who the preceding day in Quebec had been called a freemason, an enemy of the French Canadians, an imperialist, a traitor-with a profound emotion, I can still see him, the traitor to his own people and to his church; he was standing in the hall of the Seminary by the side of the Right Reverend Mathieu, archbishop of Regina. He who, according to his own people had forsaken his fellow-countrymen, and his faith, had in time of defeat and sorrow found no better place to seek solace than in Quebec Seminary by the side of that great man, the Right Reverend Mathieu.
What, may I ask our electors, the province of Quebec and our hon. friends now on the opposite side of the house for whom I have great respect, what have we promised to the province of Quebec at the last elections? What have been our promises to the province of Quebec for the last twenty years? We, of the Liberal party have promised that there would be no conscription. Yes, it is true, we have made that promise, I have made it

The Address-Mr. Bertrand (Terrebonne)
myself. When bill No. 80 was before the house, almost a majority from the province voted against conscription and most regretfully and unwillingly against their leader, the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King.
But what are we being asked to-day? What measure is before the house? We are discussing the speech from the throne, and I believe that each and every one of us appreciates the fact that in the speech from the throne there is nothing which is likely to create embarrassment nor to interfere with our political ambitions and the interest of our country. The most striking aspect of the speech from the throne are those social reforms announced by the government, their social security programme. That is the problem, Mr. Speaker, which is before the house to-day. The debate is not on conscription, nor on the question of dividing the country; it is not directed against the Province of Quebec nor against any other province. Notwithstanding the wonderful speech made by the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres in which he praised Canada's war effort, a war effort in accord with the sentiments of the Province of Quebec, the hon. member moved an amendment which comes as a surprise to everyone. For my part, I oppose this amendment though it mean the end of my political career; I represent a constituency of workers in the city of Montreal and one of the most important counties in the province; I was elected without the help of the Liberal association.
I won over the friends of the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains (Mr. Lacombe). I asked my friends what they were willing to do for this war and this is what they replied, and I think they expressed the sentiments of the province of Quebec: "We wish to do our share; we are willing to make sacrifices and work for the war; we will subscribe generously for the war effort but we are opposed to conscription."
As far as I am concerned and speaking for my electors, I may say that as long as conscription for overseas service will not be forced upon the people of this country, there will be but one leader for the constituency of Montreal-St. Mary, the province of Quebec shall never have but one leader and that leader is the present Prime Minister of Canada.
I received this morning a resolution from the Liberal Association of Montreal-St. Mary, a highly important organization since during the last election out of four candidates running three were Liberals and the other took good care not to mention that he was not a Liberal.
We, the officers of the Liberal Association of Montreal-St. Mary, gathered in a special meet-72537-42
ing, do declare unanimously that we have always had confidence in the Right Hon. Mackenzie King;
That to-day we must more than ever before be true to his policy as the only one capable of maintaining unity amongst all component parts of the country and of meeting the manifold demands of the hour;
That we have enough confidence in the patriotism of our member of parliament, Dr. Gaspard Fauteux, to give him full liberty to take the stand he deems necessary on the amendment to the amendment moved by the Hon. P. J. A. Cardin, as we are convinced that the vote he will give will be in the best interests of his country, his province and his county;
And here are some more telegrams. At the last minute, at 4125, probably learning that my name was on the list of members who were to speak this afternoon, and knowing that I had received telegrams asking me to vote for Mr. King, the Jeunes Laurentiens sent me a wire stating they hoped that I would vote against my leader. I say again to this house and to my colleagues, from Quebec that I prefer to work with Mr. King to help build a country united from coast to coast, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, than to work against him to comply with the wishes of a small group of Laurentiens who think only of their own petty interests, who seek to overthrow King as Laurier was overthrown, who attempt to overthrow another leader in Quebec as they defeated me in 1935 by resorting to slander and lies.
Mr. Speaker, with your permission and the consent of the house, I shall conclude with a sentence we love to quote in the province of Quebec, even though it was uttered by a man who was not our leader. It applies, I believe, not only to the province of Quebec, but to the whole country, and I think it is the very spirit of the policy followed by the Liberal party: " Cessons nos luttes fratricides et unis-sons-nous." Let us put a stop to our fratricidal struggles and let us unite.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have taken a great deal of interest in the amendment moved by the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin) and I am doubly interested for the simple reason that I intended, during the session, to express certain opinions along the same lines. More than once I have noted a scarcity of labour in my constituency, and since, on many occasions, the leading authorities in our country have deplored this condition, I had anticipated a debate on the question and I intended to take part in it. The sub-amendment moved by Mr. Cardin offers me an occasion to express my views on the subject, and I avail myself of this opportunity.

650	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Bertrand (Terrebonne)
During the past two weeks in particular, the information given by the members of this house, to whatever party they be long, and the complaints they have made, offer ample proof that we are faced to-day in Canada with a serious labour shortage not only in agriculture but in essential industries as well.
In my estimation, this scarcity of labour is due to the fact that recruiting in our. country has been carried on without any definite and comprehensive plan and in total ignorance of the needs of agriculture and its allied industries, as well as of the needs of other industries essential to the economic life of the nation. The raising of armies may seem all important in the eyes of the Department of National Defence, but is it possible for this department to be unmindful of the fact that armies would be helpless if, on the home front, we had no men for the production of implements of war, or to keep our communication lines open, or to extract from the soil the food products necessary to the physical life of the nation.
Agriculture is short of labour. It is asked to deliver maximum production, while on the other hand it is deprived of the necessary labour. All farmers' sons called up before or after the 23rd of March should be sent back to the land without further delay. And they should not have to go through that red tape which takes their requests from the commanding officer to the defence boards, from desk to desk, for weeks and weeks, until they get the routine answer which, no matter how important the reasons put forth, is always negative. Moreover I suggest that under the law the miller, the blacksmith and the saw-mill hands should be rated as farmers. Agriculture cannot yield sufficiently unless it has the services of those workers, especially at a time when restrictions of all kinds cripple its efforts.
Our war industries, our essential industries are also complaining of a labour shortage, which will shortly become more acute when three large plants in the Montreal district will ask for some twelve thousands of workers. War production is essential; to be efficient, it needs stable as well as skilled labour.
A number of factories have witnessed the exodus of their employees to the military camps and have been unable to replace them. Mobilization has also deprived a number of other factories-some farm implement manufacturers among them-of their skilled labour and are thereby in an embarrassing and disastrous position. It seems ridiculous to me, for instance, that expert machinists and technicians have been called for training and assigned, in military camps, to secondary jobs, while they could have been a strong element of stability and efficiency for the war effort.

I shall go even further: I claim that essential industries should be allowed to keep all the labour they need to enable them to place production on the efficient basis which will never be reached by the present ceaseless changes in their personnel.
Is it possible to attain maximum efficiency in farm and war production when, in such a vast country as ours, fast and excellent means of transportation are not available to them? Is there not a scarcity of railway employees? Do not the same conditions obtain for the motor transport companies who have to work under more and more stringent restrictions?
On November 30, 1942-about three months ago-on the occasion of the 78th general annual meeting of the shareholders of the Banque Nationale, its president, Mr. Beaudry Leman, said:
The present scarcity of labour may be due, to a certain extent, to the lack of a comprehensive plan to allocate all fit persons methodically as between the military and the economic fields. In any case, scarcity of labour is already felt in certain essential branches of production such as agriculture, stock raising, lumber operations, coal mines and even other mines which produce essential metals for the prosecution of the war. Should we not profit by England's experience, where 50,000 miners who had joined the army had to be returned to the coal mines?
Until recently, mobilization was under the Department of National War Services. To this end, the country was divided into districts headed by administrative commissions and registrars. The divisional offices were supposed to fill the requisitions for recruits, sent in by the department of National Defence, and grant postponements in accordance with a clear-cut policy. It would be unfair to say that these commissions did not try to be fair. The Montreal commission, apparently well organized, and evidently administered by a well-chosen staff, neglected nothing to attain this object. But those boards, in conformity with the instructions they had received from Ottawa, had to call for training a number of men who, if a fair plan of labour allotment had first been worked out, would greatly enhance our war effort in factories, on farms, in mines, in lumbering and in transportation.
Sooner or later, owing to the impulsion thoughtlessly given to recruiting, the labour shortage was bound to bring about the serious problem which this country is facing today. So far, nearly 800,000 men have gone into Canada's armed forces, out of a mobilizable population of 2,215,800, or one third of the latter. Now, the United States, whose population is about 140,000,000, has decided to call to arms no more than a maximum number of seven million and a half men, and a committee has just opposed the enlistment

The Address-Mr. Bertrand (Terrebonne)
of married mem, such a policy being considered by them as detrimental to the welfare of the American, nation. Canada would then make, as regards enlistments, a greater effort than the United States, which seems ridiculous. In the neighbouring country, recruiting has been conducted on a basis which kept into account the fact that industry and agriculture are two fields which in a well organized war effort should be on a par. For a few months past, the national selective service has replaced the war services in so far as mobilization is concerned. To this date has that organization achieved what was expected of it? Obviously it could not be efficiently organized without a temporary stop to recruiting, so that past errors might be corrected and a new labour allotment plan worked out for the benefit of the various phases of our war effort. To date, our man-power has been almost thoughtlessly requisitioned, as if that were the only important factor in achieving a war effort. If the present situation continues, the economic life of this country will be threatened. If production of war supplies should decrease, if transportation facilities should be curtailed through a labour shortage or a lack of materials caused by a labour shortage, would our war effort be enhanced? If agricultural production should lag, on account of a labour shortage, would that place our war effort on a better footing? This labour problem must be faced or it will cause irreparable clefts in the economic structure of our nation.
In the speech he delivered at the meeting to which I have just referred, Mr. Beaudry Leman made this important statement which speaks for itself:
War expenditures for the present fiscal year will reach nearly $4,000,000,000. This figure shows the magnitude of our economic effort, but it also emphasizes the burden which has to be borne by a country of eleven million and a half people, a nation which wants to be, at one and the same time, a granary, an arsenal and a man-power reservoir. Now the leaders of the united nations tell us about a war of attrition which might last for a few more years. We ought to remember that "slow and steady wins the race."
In order to win the peace after a war of attrition, there should be left reserves of manpower, capital, foodstuffs, raw materials and products of every description. Influence in world affairs will pass from those countries which will have to ask for assistance to those which will be in a position to tender assistance.
Furthermore, the power of a belligerent country depends in a large measure on the balance between its war-time economy and its peace-time economy, for a loss of balance might give rise to serious results. An excessive effort, untimely or misdirected, disturbing the national economy which is its basis, might weaken Can-72537- 42J
ada before the end of hostilities. After the war, our country will be unable to assume the heavy responsibilities which will be devolved upon it, if its economic position is not sound and secure.
I am not opposed to the war effort of my country as witnessed by my attitude in the past. I feel that, in a war which has developed into a world war, Canada upholds the principles of democracy as well as a civilization based upon the fear of God and regard for human freedom. I am not opposed to our war effort; I have done more in my constituency than any member in this house has done in his own to help the government solve its war-time industrial problems. I am not opposed to our war effort, but if it is shown that, at the present time, Canada is doing more, in relation to its population, than any other country, am I not right in assuming that there must be a limit to its effort and that this limit has already been reached? If such talk brands me an isolationist, I welcome the name. However, I look upon other nations of the empire. Has not Eire asserted her neutrality? Did South Africa impose conscription? Is not her war effort limited to the confines of the African continent? As for New Zealand and Australia, are they not waging war within circumscribed areas and have they not clearly defined their position? Isolationists? No; but Canadians for short, that's the word. Descendants of this country's first settlers, we set Canada above all other countries. Allowances we have made aplenty since the war's outbreak. The province of Quebec has made more indeed than any other province and I need not give details. If Canada can boast of national unity, or of anything like it, let us not seek afar for the reason: it has come out almost entirely of the allowances made by the province of Quebec.
These few words, Mr. Speaker, have enabled me to express my views. I have done so without mental reservation, with the sincerity of which I feel possessed and with no thought of personal advantage. I don't know how long I shall remain in politics but, so long as I am here, I mean to say what I believe to be fair. On February 8 last, I said I continued to sit on this side of the house because I am afforded freedom of speech or of utterance. I wonder now if this freedom still exists after the speech delivered by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) Friday afternoon. During my address on February 8, I conceded the Prime Minister's special abilities as a leader and admired the prestige he enjoys in the United States, with whom after the war, Canada, an American country, will be called upon to assume a leading role. I did say
The Address-Division

nonetheless that, on all measures that come before the house, I will vote as my conscience dictates; and, in the present debate, duty compels me to support the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before proceeding with ray comments on the amendment to the main motion I should like to say a very few words about the situation created last Friday by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). He made certain remarks concerning the numerous parties formed lately throughout Canada. To a certain extent I think his remarks are quite right, but I wish to remind him that those newly-formed political parties have all arisen under his regime. Some of them have been formed right from the. ranks of the Liberal party.
The Prime Minister also made reference to the rivalry existing among different opposition members in the house. Well, with regard to that I would point out that the most typical example of political rivalry we have seen in the House of Commons was at the conclusion of the debate on Bill No. 80 of last session, to amend the National Resources Mobilization Act, 1940, when the Prime Minister himself replied to the then leader of the opposition, the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson). The Prime Minister said also that the opposition lodged against the government was to serve some political aims and ambitions.
We from Quebec know what was said and done in our province during the twenty-five years prior to the provincial election of 1939 and the federal election in March, 1940. We know the promises that were made in Quebec during that period. Those promises were such that the Prime Minister was obliged to hold a plebiscite to be released from them, and that cost the country nearly 82,000,000 of public money. That was political ambition, and the Prime Minister should be the last one to talk to others about political ambitions.
The amendment moved by the Conservatives has been read in the house so many times that I shall dispense with having hon. members listen to it again. It looks to me like a soft pedal on the policy of the Conservative party in the past. The Winnipeg convention was held this winter, and since that time speeches have ben made by the new leader of the party, Mr. Bracken. Those speeches have been made in such a form as to give an impression to the population of Canada that the Conservative party was putting a soft pedal on its imperialistic policies. We have heard two speeches in the house, one by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon), which dealt in considerable detail with the man-power shortage faced by war industries and agriculture. Then the former leader of the opposition, the hon. member for York-Sunbury, said
that the people of this country were more heavily taxed than the people of the United States or Great Britain.. Hearing those speeches I thought the party had changed its imperialistic policies; I thought it was no more in favour of a greater war effort than the Liberal party was making. However there appears to have been some change in this late policy. There is a saying that what is bred in the bone will come out in the flesh. Last Friday, answering a speech by the Prime Minister, the leader of the opposition said this, as reported on page 562 of Hansard:
In the months that lie ahead we shall need reinforcements for our army. Let us, as a parliament and as a country, not leave any doubt in the minds of those fighting with us in this great war for freedom; let us not permit the word to go forth that we are not ready to do everything that may be necessary with respect to man-power, financial resources and all things that will bring forth a total war effort in this dominion.
That completes the amendment. Now that that has been said, we know more of what to think about the amendment. The leader of the opposition continued:
It is true that our own amendment is a vote of want of confidence in the government, but it is founded on grounds that we think will make for a greater war effort in Canada instead of a lesser one, as would be the case if the hon. gentleman's amendment should carry.
If that is the aim of the amendment, we now know exactly what to think about it.
At the conclusion of my remarks I intend to move an amendment which will also be a motion of want of confidence in the government. It is to replace and improve the one which has already been offered, and I hope the Prime Minister will be satisfied with it.
First of all, I should like to say something about the shortage of man-power throughout Canada.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: In your new party?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
You will hear more about the
new party after the next election. Many of you will hear about it, but from seats different from those you now occupy.
As I say, I intend to move an amendment at the conclusion of my remarks. Most of the hon. members who have taken part in this debate have referred to the man-power shortage that exists at the present time. I wonder how one can ask for a greater war effort and still criticize or complain about the man-power situation. I know that in the past the Conservative party have never brought about any great miracles and perhaps they think if they were in power they could bring one about that would supply to industry and agriculture all the man-power that is needed, and at the same time continue the
The Address-Mr. Roy

drafting of men; that would be a wonderful miracle, but I do not think they will have a chance to bring it about.
There is without doubt a shortage of manpower. All the speeches we have heard in the house testify to such a shortage. In order to prevent it there is only one thing to do-and that is why I voted in favour of the amendment of the hon. member for Richelieu-Ver-cheres (Mr. Cardin)-we must stop the drafting of recruits throughout Canada. There are but three places where our man-power can be found. One is the army and the other two are the war industries and the farms. If there is already a shortage of man-power and the army continues to draft men from the other two sources, the problem will increase. I do not think anyone can bring about a miracle to change the effect of this wrong procedure.
In spite of all that has been said about us we are for victory. That is why last year I joined with the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains (Mr. Lacombe) in moving an amendment to exempt from military service all men employed on the farm in order to permit the vital industry of agriculture to carry on with a production which is most necessary to our war effort. I cannot understand why hon. members should support a government which follows such a rash policy When the government needed additional employees for its own civil service, it did not let those employees go into the army. The civil service has been increased by about 70,000 men and women. However, when agriculture, which is the basis of the war effort for our allies, is concerned, the government does not deal with it in the same way. It did not proceed as it did to meet the needs of the civil service or the other needs of government in connection with various organizations. It went right ahead and took the skilled manpower, that cannot now be replaced. It took so many men that to-day every hon. member, including even those who have not expressed their opinions in this house, believes there is a shortage of labour on our farms. If we do not have an abundant crop next fall; if the season is not as good as it was last year, and if we lack labour to cultivate the farms, we may find ourselves in very great misery before very long, and our war effort will suffer as a result.
As I have said already, no miracle will happen to give us more labour on our farms and in our war industries. There is only one way to correct the situation, namely, to stop this policy of drafting men which has gone far beyond the limits of our mathematical capacity. In my opinion the way to stop such a

policy is this. Conscription must be applied to those financiers who are making as much more money as there are more soldiers in the army, or who are making as much more money as there are more contracts coming to war industries. Those people will stop making money out of the army and out of our war effort when they are compelled to take the money out of their own pockets to help win the war. Then, as I said in a previous speech, their advice will become much wiser.
I should like now to deal with another matter, and I wish I had a far better knowledge of English in order to do so, for it would be much easier to keep from making any slips of the tongue, as it is said in English, and to avoid hurting the feelings of anyone. It should be well understood that the complaint I have to make about a certain gentleman or a certain little organization does not in our opinion involve all our Anglo-Saxon fellow Canadians. We know them far too well for that. We remember what was done for us by great statesmen like Baldwin, MacNab, Macdonald and a great many others, and we would not want to. hurt the feelings of any person or any group, but this is a very particular case with which I wish to deal. I hold in my hand a publication entitled the Gospel Witness and Protestant Advocate. The editor is Reverend T. T. Shields, and I should like to read a few extracts from this fine example of literature which seems to be founded upon a hatred of all Catholics in regard to our war effort in Canada. First I would refer to the issue of October 22, 1942, at page 2:
The Roman Catholic Cardinal "will assume the responsibility of settling the whole matter." This is the man who has been recently honoured by Queen's university. It seems to us that if the devil himself would only appear in the robes of a cardinal-and it must be admitted that in this cardinal he has an excellent representative-universities, city councils, Canadian clubs and empire clubs, the dominion cabinet and the Canadian premier himself would all bow down to him.
Then a little further along he says:
That is Roman Catholicism-as deadly a poison to the individual, to the family, to evangelical Christianity and to the state- indeed a more deadly poison than the germ of typhus, or tuberculosis, or smallpox, or leprosy, or the black plague.
That is what this gentleman has to say about the Catholic religion. Then in the issue of June 25, 1942, this review reproduces an article from the Victoria Daily Times of Monday, June 22, reporting a speech made by Mr. Shields somewhere out west. The article states:
Roman Catholicism was the enemy of free institutions everywhere, he said. It was the fourth axis power and just as much the implacable enemy of Britain as Germany, Italy

The Address-Mr. Roy
and Japan, he added remarking, Though we win the war the chief enemy will still be in the Vatican.
The real ruler of Canada this moment is not Prime Minister Mackenzie King, but Cardinal Villeneuve of Quebec, he said. Not a thing could be done without approval from the Vatican, he added.
Doctor Shields told his hearers one of the reasons R. B. Bennett left Canada lay in his weariness of having the Roman Catholic church continually pulling his coat-tails for special privileges.
In the November 12, 1942, issue of the same publication appears an article entitled "The Relative Importance of Unity," which concludes in this way:
In religious controversies we have repeatedly seen errorist minorities numerically overwhelmed, only to observe an organized subtilty defeat a superior number of unaffiliated individualist advocates of righteousness.
All this is another way of saying, Beware of peace. In these colunms we have repeatedly pointed to that religio-politieo thing called the papacy as the chief of all visible enemies of mankind. As the tide of battle turns and the doom of the axis powers becomes visibly nearer, we may expect the papacy, gradually and without announcement, to abandon its neutrality, and endeavour to ingratiate itself with the powers of freedom. We must not allow ourselves to feel the slightest elation when gangsters begin to cheer the police. As the tide gradually turns in our favour and against the axis, we may expect to see the whole Roman Catholic hierarchy in Canada emulate the example of Admiral Darlan: they will fight even openly just so long as they think there is any chance of winning, but as soon as they see the die is cast, they will make their exit from France, and turn up as a guest of the victorious armies. Therefore, wrhile we are far from the end_ of the conflict, the Quislings who helped to precipitate it will soon be attempting to reorient themselves in order to get as much out of the wreck they have made, as may be possible.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. What I have just read is quite clear; we can see that the reverend gentleman becomes more than saucy. He becomes somewhat dangerous. It would be easy for the government to stop this sort of propaganda. Again, in the Victoria Daily Times of Monday, June 22, 1942, Doctor Shields is reported thus:
"I don't believe the Roman Catholic Church need be feared after the war," he added. It was the most gigantic bluffer in the world. Its forces would fight in ambush and darkness, "but when you turn the light on it, it runs," he said.
He denied any personal quarrel with individual Roman Catholics, but said sometimes "in exposing the ravages of Rome some Roman Catholics may get a few splinters of shrapnel."
Is that what he wants-a sort of bloody persecution against the Catholics? He does not
put to himself this question: Are the French-Canadians or the Catholics in Quebec being treated fairly in this war effort? Are they getting the same wages in the war industries in Quebec as workers in similar industries in Ontario? Does he ask himself, when our boys are sent to Hong Kong, Dieppe, or elsewhere, whether they are Catholics or not? No; this gentleman does not worry about conditions that exist in Quebec or about what Quebec is doing in spite of the unfair treatment we are at present receiving.
There is another matter I would draw to the attention of the government. This issue of October 22, 1942, of the Gospel Witness from which I have quoted, and which at the time of the last victory loan seemed to circulate to the extent of a good many thousands of copies, contained on the back page a cartoon, showing in the centre the church of St. Peter of Rome, with the armorial bearings of the pope at the top, and showing at either side of the church Mussolini and Hitler making a salute to the church of Rome. Written -in big letters, so big, Mr. Speaker, that you can see them from your place, are these words, "The Relationship of Roman Catholicism to Nazi-Fascism." This pamphlet was distributed among the English-speaking population of our country at the time of the last victory loan in October. At the same time there was distributed throughout the whole province of Quebec another pamphlet, in French only-according to the information I could secure from the bureau of information-and on the front cover is a photograph of the interior of a Catholic church in which a service is proceeding. There is written at the bottom, in French, "Us Veulent Detruire l'Eglise de Dieu", which means in English, "They want to destroy the Church of God". That is referring to Hitler and Mussolini. On the back, to give this publication the appearance of another religious pamphlet which is also published in Quebec under the name of "Le Messager du Sacre-Coeur", there is printed a picture of the Sacred Heart with these words below, in French, "Je suis la Voie, la Verite et la Vie", which means in English, "I am the Way, the Truth, and the Life". Inside the booklet will be found pictures of Hitler. His portrait is close to that of Cardinal Villeneuve; and the statement of Cardinal Villeneuve in favour of our war effort and against the axis powers appears under the portrait of Hitler. This booklet was published by the Service of Information, Ottawa, under the authorization of Hon. J. T. Thor-son, Minister of National War Services. This was circulated in Quebec at the very same

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
time that the other review from which I have quoted was circulated among English-speaking Canadians in other parts of the country. This one that was circulated in the province of Quebec was published by the government's own bureau of information. I wonder which one of these gives the truth? I do not know. But I want to say to you, Mr. Speaker, that this kind of propaganda throughout the country is not only false, but lowers respect for religious beliefs. It is against the unity of Canadians; it is against the best interests of our war effort, and it should be condemned. Since the government has permitted the circulation of this review and at the same time has published this other pamphlet which has been circulated in Quebec province, I say that the attitude of the government in both instances is wrong, and that we should stop this business.
I should like to speak English well enough to appeal to the spirit of fair play and- justice of all the members of this house and to the respect which I am sure every hon. member has for the religious belief held by Catholics throughout Canada. I appeal to my fellow-members to support our country in which all serious-minded men are willing to work to help win this war, for which purpose we are asked to vote huge sums of money. I also ask the government to stop this kind of propaganda which is nothing else but forgeries and rashness.
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Dorion):
That all the words after the words "Your advisers have" in the amendment be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"not taken the necessary measures to stop the present anti-Catholic propaganda and prevent the circulation of some abusive publications conflicting with the purposes enunciated at the time of our war declarations and contrary at the same time to the spirit of the confederation pact and of the Atlantic charter, and, further, the rural and labour populations of the dominion are not adequately represented among Your Excellency's advisers and that this deficiency is responsible for the inequitable application of the National Resources Mobilization Act."

I did) not wish to interrupt him when he was speaking, but I do not wish a certain statement he made to go unchallenged because it is wholly incorrect. My hon. friend, as I understood him, referring to third parties in this house, said that they had come into being during the course of the administration of this country's affairs by a government 
of which I had the honour to be the head. Looking at the third parties in the house, I recognize first the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. My recollection is, and I think I am right, that the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation came into being at the convention which was held in Regina in 1932 or 1933.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

The convention was held, I believe, in 1933, when the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett was the leader of the Conservative party and the Conservative party were in office. I look beyond, and see another third party, the Social Credit party. My recollection is that that party also came into being between 1930 and 1935. I believe that Mr. Aberhart in his province came into power in the early summer of 1935, and that the first Social Credit candidates who offered themselves for the federal house did so in 1935. So that that party came into being during the time when the former Prime Minister, Mr. Bennett, was leading the Conservative party in this house and that party was in power.
I come to another party, the Progressive Conservative party. It has come, it is true, into being in the time during which this administration has been in office, but I think I can safely say that the Progressive Conservative party is the same old Conservative party, under another name.
As for the remaining parties, so-called, I do not think they are so much parties as they are leaders and would-be leaders of parties.
I hope that my hon. friend will see that I am seeking only to correct him, but I think it is advisable that the correction should be made.

speechtext: I merely wanted to say this to the Prime Minister, with all seriousness and gravity. I suggest to him that in the course of this debate, at a time when he himself has said that this country, and indeed the whole world, are facing grave issues, requiring our serious consideration and our urgent attention, these old questions of how many parties grew up, and when, could be appropriately left until such time as victory has been won.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words with reference to the amendment to the amendment of the member for Gaspe as to what he calls "abusive publications". Freedom of religion is something which the British, empire and the mother country have had since time immemorial. This is the greatest war the world has ever seen. Its importance, is primary, not secondary. While I believe in freedom of religion I believe also that this parliament should stick to its task of attending to the war; and let me say that there is no province which has more to fear to-day from at least one aspect of that war, the sinkings around our coasts, than the province of Quebec.
A great many people do not agree with some of these papers. All my life I have been a warm friend of the Catholic people of the city of which I was the head. There is no bigotry in Toronto; it is a tolerant place. If we are to set ourselves up as a sort of religious parliament and take into consideration every pamphlet which is published on either side, we shall be doing something which we have no right to do. The matter is one of property and civil rights, within the jurisdiction of the provinces, and in dealing with it this parliament is going very far afield.
The amendment to the amendment also brings in the Atlantic charter. Well, Casablanca put the Atlantic charter in the waste-paper basket the other day.
Many matters which are not in order have been discussed in this chamber. Let me say to the hon. gentleman who moved the amendment to the amendment that I have a warm regard for him, but I fail to see what we,
sitting here as a parliament, have to do with religion. All of us, Jew and Gentile, black and white,, should be equal before the law, and subject to the law every person is free to express his opinions. A great many of the matters which are referred to were virtually forgotten long before the last war, at least by a large number of the people of this country, and why they should be reopened at this time I do not know. I recall that the Rev. Mr. Toplady, who wrote that great hymn, "Rock of Ages," was in his time one of the most violent controversialists in. behalf of certain religious opinions. Those doctrines and dogmas are forgotten to-day, but his hymn written in 1836, has brought comfort to the sick and dying the world over, while his religious controversies were long ago forgotten. I believe, with war on, that we should leave these disputes alone. We must think of such matter as the sinkings in the gulf of St. Lawrence; of the fact that five hundred ships sent to North Africa, with three hundred and fifty men-of-war and one hundred and twenty escorts, have been removed from the north Atlantic; that General Winter that has been the best friend we have had in the St. Lawrence, will not continue to aid us much longer. We had better stick to our own business. It is for the provinces, controlling property and civil rights, to regulate this issue. There is a law of libel, and if there is anything libellous in these articles the courts are available to determine the question; it should not be brought before parliament. .
I protest against an amendment of this kind, dealing with a purely religious controversy of which people know little or nothing, very few having even read these pamphlets. I believe in freedom of religion and freedom of thought. I have heard a great many controversies and I do not agree with most of the controversialists on either side. I am a humble member of the church of England. That church believes in freedom of religion and freedom of speech. In any event we are wasting our time, for this is a subject beyond our powers. If you ask me, sir, the amendment to the amendment should be ruled out of order as dealing with something which lies within the jurisdiction of the provinces under section 91 of the British North America Act. If there is any grievance, let those who complain of it go to Queen's Park, which authorizes the publication of pamphlets. I repeat that I object to this parliament being made the scene of a religious controversy which is none of our business.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I seconded the amendment to the amendment moved by the hon. member for
The Address-Mr. Lacombe

Gaspe (Mr. Roy) just as I would second any amendment moved in the public interest. It is indeed regrettable to view religious quarrels brought about by fanatics who should be excluded from our society. It is a known fact that a certain clergyman in Toronto is constantly attacking the Roman Catholic religion by his speeches and his articles. This gentleman even sends to hon. members of this house his publication. Does he know how insulted we feel when we receive his paper? The Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) is vested with all the necessary powers to stop this propaganda, which affects more than four million Canadians. The attitude taken by Rever-'end Shields is a cause of scandal in a country which more than ever should attempt to maintain harmony. On many occasions municipal authorities have had to intervene in order to stop this man from spreading doubt, dissension and discord. The clergyman from Jarvis street causes trouble not only in the province of Quebec, but from the Atlantic to the Pacific. A bishop from British Columbia had to appeal to the Minister of Justice to prevent this man from repeating in his diocese his insults against the Roman Catholic church. This state of matters must cease and the government should take action in that regard without further delay.
The amendment to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Gaspe deals with the readjustment of salaries for Canadian workers. This measure is urgent, and I know that the working class of Quebec is entitled to a just reward for its labour to the same extent as workers in the other provinces. Let us take the farm labour problem. As I have already said very often in this house, if the government does not grant complete exemption from military training to farmers and farm hands we shall be headed for disaster and starvation. Furthermore, all farmers actually undergoing their military training should be sent back to their farms. The hon. member for Gaspe is perfectly right in deploring the fact that farmers and labourers are not adequately represented in the cabinet. This is the reason why so many people in this country are exploited by the trusts. While farmers, labourers and craftsmen are working, toiling and suffering, war profiteers are reaping public funds. This deplorable situation must cease.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) does not seem to be pleased with the new parties. At least this was the opinion he expressed with unusual strength on February 19. He said that multiplicity of parties was responsible for the downfall of France. This was not the determining factor of the defeat of that great country, and the Prime Minister

knows it. One must go further back in history, to the point where the victorious allies of the last great war began losing the peace when they were preparing the treaty of Versailles. If France was in a state of extreme weakness when the present war broke out, it was as a result of the guilty complacency of the victor much more than of the formation of new political parties in that country. Who allowed the Rhineland to be remilitarized a few years before Stanley Baldwbn stated that the first line of defence of Great Britain was on the Rhine? The unquenchable financial and commercial imperialism of certain nations was responsible for the downfall of France to a greater extent than was the creation of new political groups.
During the last war a few people grew rich while others suffered untold hardships. A few loathsome profiteers flooded Europe with war equipment. Boundaries did not exist for cannon merchants. The ocean itself was no barrier for those ever greedy madmen, the most active and at the same time the most repulsive of whom was Sir Basil Zaharoff. Holder of a baronetcy, commander of the order of the bath and grand officer of the legion of honour, that shady character became the intimate friend of the great political and military men of that period. He gave advice on war operations; he travelled from one seaport to another in perfect safety; he laid down the law, and compelled those in power to obey him. In short, he dominated governments and influenced history.
The terrible and horrible war which engulfed the lives of sixty thousand of our countrymen on foreign battlefields, which cost and is still costing us billions, which cost thirty-three countries the staggering sum of $186,000,000,000, and in which fifteen million men were killed, now appears to have been useless and to have settled nothing. Why? Simply because Germany, though she may have lost the war, won a great peace-time victory through the failure of the other powers to realize the inevitable consequences of their actions. When Germany was condemned to pay reparations a few of the victors proved quite willing to grant her loans much more considerable than the amounts she had to pay. When her commercial fleet was seized her enemies of yesterday provided her with the funds required to build another and more powerful one. Dictatorship of money; what crimes we commit in your name! Twenty-five years ago the old Germany was crushed and begging for mercy. To-day the new Germany, in a shaken Europe, openly defies the democracies. Behind the back of the League of Nations she imposed humiliating

The Address-Mr. Pouliot
conditions on Great Britain and France. What happened when the vanquished of yesterday demanded the dismemberment of Czechoslovakia? Two great nations gave way in the face of the terrible doctrine, "Might is right".
These are indeed cruel truths, but no purpose is to be served by concealing them. It is far better to turn the searchlight of truth on the lowest strata of international life. In the face of events like these, invisible forces such as cooperation and love of peace remain the only safeguards of our civilization. The petty interests and criminal hypocrisy of certain nations have led all peoples into the terrible situation which now confronts us. To ensure the peace and progress of the world should have been the ultimate goal of the statesmen who were called upon to guide the destinies of the most powerful countries on earth; but arbitration and conciliation treaties were wrecked by a formidable instrument, 'that of financial and military imperialism. As substitutes for disarmament, tranquillity and the free development of peoples, heinous psychological trends have given us all the devilish weapons invented by a barbarism which we still dare to clothe with the noble name of civilization. Even Winston Churchill raised loud protests at Westminster in 1938 and 1939 against the criminal complacency shown by financiers of all kinds who continued to lend Germany enormous sums of money in order to facilitate the rebuilding of her navy. Right here in Canada a few weeks and even a few days before the present war broke out, shameful trusts were shipping to the enemy large quantities of nickel, rubber, steel, oil and gasoline. With heroic Belgium and Holland, heroic France, my mother country, was the first to fall under the blows of a formidable war machine which past and present allies had built up for Germany. No; France did not succumb to the quarrels of a few new political parties who were rather harmless. France was defeated by the shameful betrayal of commercial, military and financial imperialism. When history is written the impartial historian will strike out that page which the Prime Minister wrote on February 19, 1943, on the deep causes of the fall of France.
In conclusion, I would formulate this wish. National unity will live in Canada inasmuch as our living strength is preserved from disaster by a sound political economy. Where are we going in this whirlwind of billions succeeding other billions? Where are we heading with this mad race on public funds? What will become of our agriculture, our industries, our trade? In what society are we living? The future is so dark that I foresee
the disintegration of our families and the bewilderment of our population, with generations of Canadians toiling under the burden of excessive taxation. I am thinking at present of the state of decadence and bankruptcy which will fall upon us as a consequence of our participation in this war on a scale out of all proportion to our resources, and I sincerely hope that God may' preserve us from such a calamity. Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, I will vote for the amendment to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Gaspe.
Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): Before the vote is taken I have just a few words to say with regard to censorship. There was a great man who was in charge of the censors in Great Britain at the beginning of the war. He was Lord Macmillan, and he stated his views on the general rules of censorship in this way:
Lord Macmillan sensibly gave orders to the censors that they are to confine their activities to news of a military character likely to be of value to the enemy, and are to refrain from censoring matter which merely happens to be politically disagreeable to the British government.
I take this from The Week, September 20, 1939, just at the beginning of the war.
This is a very reasonable view. It is a view which is in accordance with British usage. I do not discuss the qualifications of the head of the Canadian bureau of censors, who is supposed to be a counsel of certain fame; but what I cannot understand is the laxity of censorship regarding yellow-press news, such as the publicity stunt afforded by the trial of Errol Flynn. Some incidents in his trial were simply disgusting. Then, there was the story of Frances Farmer who was always drunk; it was one which could not be accepted as an example for either the young or the old.
It takes a great deal of courage to bring the case of Pastor Shields before the house, on account of the blackmail Shields uses at all times against those who dare to criticize him. I do not know whether or not I am right, but according to my information his case was to be considered-or was considered. I would direct the attention of the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) to some Quebec jurisprudence respecting the rights of minorities. It is a very old case in which a man-and I do not recall whether he was a notary or a journalist -named Plamondon was sued by a Quebec Jew who complained that the defendant had written articles which had the effect of dissuading clients from buying at the plaintiff's store, simply because he was a Jew. I do not remember the decision of the superior court, but I have a distinct recollection of the judgment
The Address-Mr. Pouliot

rendered by the court of appeal, which was headed by no less a person than the late Sir Horace Archambault, then chief justice of the province of Quebec. That judgment stated that any man guilty of such offence against a citizen belonging to a minority in the province should pay a considerable amount of money. That is Quebec jurisprudence.
Now that most of the civil powers of the province have been taken by the federal government, I wonder that no distinction is made between freedom of speech and abuse. I did have some observations to make respecting the address in reply, and perhaps this would be a good time to make them. The amendment to the amendment of the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Roy) refers to the Atlantic charter. Well and good. I am all for the Atlantic charter. It will be remembered that four freedoms were mentioned in that charter, the first two of which were freedom from fear and freedom from want. Those two appear in the speech from the throne as it is contained at page 3 of the Votes and Proceedings of this session. But to my great astonishment the speech from the throne does not mention the other two freedoms, which are just as great and just as necessary in any democracy as are freedom from fear and freedom from want. I refer to freedom of speech and freedom of religion. They are not mentioned in the speech from the throne. Why? Let hon. members now sitting in the house check the record. I was astounded when I noted that omission.
I have another regret to express, namely, that there no distinction is made between freedom and licence. Freedom of speech and licence of speech are not at all the same thing. Freedom of speech is the right to say anything which is not against good order in the country. Licence is the procedure of saying things which may be injurious to public safety and order. I sincerely believe that what Shields has said from the pulpit is dangerous to good government, good order and peace in this country. So much is this so that two of the largest hotels in Canada-the finest hotel in Ottawa, the Chateau Laurier, and one of the largest in Montreal, the Windsor-have refused Pastor Shields the right to repeat an address in which he called the Roman Catholic church the fifth column in Canada. The authorities at the Chateau Laurier are officials under the control of the Canadian National Railways, and certainly the board of directors of the Windsor hotel at Montreal are not bigoted men. However, the officials of both those hotels felt they could not admit this man Shields to repeat under their roofs that which

was injurious to large numbers of our fellow citizens. Their understanding was the same as that of the King's Bench which was presided over by the late Sir Horace Archambault on a different occasion, namely, that minority rights in this country shall be respected.
We hear a great deal about national unity. One thing I regret very deeply is that some people take for granted that Canadians of British origin necessarily think differently from Canadians of other origins. That is a great mistake. The troublemakers in this country are a very small minority. I have had the privilege of travelling in Ontario and in the maritimes, although I have not been so fortunate as to have done the same through the west, but I shall do it soon. The people of Ontario whom I know and the people of the maritimes whom I know, whether of British origin or of French origin, think the same when they consider anything without religious or race prejudice. They are all vgood people. There are, however, certain people who are interested in having this country disunited. They are only a few, but they do this to prevent the Canadian people from being informed of what they are doing. These troublemakers are the war profiteers who control the press through their advertisements.
One of my regrets is that there is not an independent English daily press in this country to give the proper information to the Canadian people. Recently I was in a large Canadian city where two evening papers are published. I bought both papers and they could be r.ead in five minutes, or possibly in three or two minutes. There were just a few headlines on the front pages, some newS, and then advertisements for the women who wanted to go to the stores to buy food or clothing or other commodities. I made a comparison between those large fat papers and the weekly press.
Why is our daily press not just as good as the average weekly press? The weekly press publishes some advertisements, but the editors are close to the farmer; they take time to think and they show more independence. I do not know whether the publication referred to by the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Roy) was monthly or weekly; since I do not read it I do not know what it is. I have listened to the quotations he gave. It is deplorable that papers with the largest circulation among the English people are quite often-there are a few happy exceptions-much below the average of the weekly press.
Speaking again of censorship, what I have to say will be quite brief. The other day I wanted some information about our trade but

The Address-Mr. Pouliot
I could not get it because the censor held it up. If any horn, member will look at our trade publications he will see that they contain practically no information. We are told that our exports are larger than they were before. This may be true because I do not know whether my information is correct, but I have been told that the total amount of our exports includes the gifts we have made to other countries. This is absurd, if true.
It is also impossible to get any information about importations from Great Britain. Why? Is it because the minister of trade of Great Britain said when he was in Canada last year that they could supply us with any merchandise we wanted? Is it because our exports at the present time are mostly war munitions, food, grain and lumber? Is it forbidden by the censor that members of parliament be given detailed information about our exports because our imports from Great Britain are entirely different from our exports, being made up mainly of commercial merchandise? If that is the situation there is no reason why this information should be refused. It would not help the enemy to know what kind of merchandise we are getting from Great Britain provided it is not war munitions and arms. That is why I express my feeling about this matter.
We are doing our best to help the common cause; we are all for it. But is it not time to follow the example of Great Britain and produce merchandise for export like that country is doing although it is exposed to bombardment? That is one question. If we do not do that, what will be our external trade when the war is over? We shall be left without any trade at all. It is time to think of that. Many people are employed to-day. They do their work happily. They make money; so much the better for them. But we must think of the aftermath and see to it that all good examples which are given by the old country are followed by us.
