I am sorry I have to speak a little louder for my hon. friend. I have expressed my views on these matters, and I think my hon. friend the member for Gaspe was right in bringing them to the attention of the house.
But there is something more. I have heard from a source which I cannot give that when Mr. Chaloult was prosecuted, Pastor Shields was also to be prosecuted. Then it was not Pastor Shields who was prosecuted; it was Mr. Drew. Then the charge was withdrawn. I have also been informed that it was a Roman Catholic from another province than
that of Quebec who intervened to stop all prosecutions against Pastor Shields. Did he act for himself or on the suggestion of some other gentleman? Although I cannot disclose the source of my information, I can say that it is generally pretty good. If the government had really considered the case of Pastor Shields and decided that he should be prosecuted, why did they change Shields for Drew? That I cannot understand, because they do not belong to the same church, and their cases are entirely different. By the way, Mr. Chaloult was acquitted, and so was Mr. Decary of Montreal, who was the registrar of the National war services board. He was accused before the courts and suffered calumny, and then he was acquitted by the Supreme Court of Canada. I was humiliated as a French-Canadian when I saw the way in which those gentlemen were treated, but I was most indignant when I saw the way in which the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Gauthier) was dealt with. When a charge is laid against an officer there is a previous investigation and all the charges are summarized. Therefore the army authorities know in advance the charge in the case. What I complain bitterly of is this, and I would say the same if it had been any Conservative member or any Jewish member or any citizen of Canada: Here was this man, a member of the House of Commons, put in custody, in gaol, if you wish, for fifty-one days, during which time the worst calumnies were circulated against him. Some one sent me some clippings from papers from all over the country, papers from British Columbia, for instance, with headings in type about two or three inches high, " Quebec Scandal." It was portrayed as a Quebec scandal. That is what happens every time when it is a case in the province of Quebec.
I have the best possible disposition toward this government, not toward all the members of the government, but especially towards the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), for whom I have been fighting for years; but I tell you, Mr. Speaker, that if those things had been done by a Tory government, the Liberal party would have been one to fight it. How can we speak of freedom when these things happen? It was the reverse of the British practice. In Britain a man is considered innocent, or not guilty, until he is found guilty. In the case of the hon. member for Portneuf, it was known in advance by the national defence department that the charge against him could not be substantiated. Nevertheless the brass hats decided to humiliate him by keeping him for fifty-one days in the "clink" at the citadel. Not only that, but gossip-I know it is untrue-went on and
The Address-Mr. Pouliot

on, and even members of the cabinet were associated in the calumnies that were made against the hon. member. I protested each time very strongly. But that is what was done. It is not only as a Roman Catholic, not only as a French Canadian from the province of Quebec, but as a Canadian, that I protest against the abuses I have mentioned which appeared in the Gospel Witness and the abuses of which the brass hats in Ottawa have been guilty, and so on and so on. It is as a Canadian I protest, a Canadian who has never raised a racial or a religious issue in this house. I have always abstained from doing so, but I think this sort of thing should stop. Of course, there are some people who live by it. But now that people throughout the' country are showing a spirit of magnanimity in this war, I hope that all this which has to be regretted will not happen again and will not have to be deplored again. These things would not happen if the proper distinction were made between licence of speech and freedom of speech, and if the government were ready to assume their responsibilities when it is time to do so. Sometimes it is not necessary to assume any responsibility; yet they tell us, "Well, we have assumed a great responsibility". This time I must remind my good friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) that he has at his disposal all the machinery which is necessary to stop this; and I will tell also the Minister of National War Services (Mr. LaFleehe) that he must give definite instructions to the censor to censor news which should not appear in the press, and also comments which are prejudicial to the good understanding that must exist in this country.
I have been very mild in my remarks. Before closing, as I do not want to make another speech on this address, I have just a word to say to the hon. member for Belle-chasse (Mr. Picard). I listened to him this afternoon; he is an able speaker. I know that for many years he was the secretary of the late Mr. Lapointe, and he was of a good enough disposition quite often to speak on my behalf in my constituency. I know him well enough to tell him that I was very sorry regarding what he said of the late Mr. Lapointe, who was a very dear friend of mine. As he knows, Mr. Lapointe and I were on the best possible terms, and I always regarded him as a big brother. I will say no more about him because his remembrance is in the hearts of all those who have known him. What Mr. Lapointe had to say in his lifetime he said, and I believe that hon. members know enough of the good relations which existed-

speechtext:
I had not intended to speak on this amendment, but, having regard to what has been said in the course of the debate thus far, it is important, I think, that I should draw the attention of the house and the country to the possible consequences of continuing the debate and permitting a motion of this kind to go to a division.

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
There are times and places for all things. The hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), who has just taken his seat, said that he thought it was well that the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Roy) should have brought this subject to the attention of the house. I take no exception to his bringing any subject to the attention of the house, but I take very strong exception to the hon. member bringing the subject in the form of a motion of ^ant of confidence in the administration, bringing it on the address, and raising for discussion in the house at this particular time a subject which cannot be other than perhaps the most controversial of any which could be raised at this time of war.
On grounds of public policy I am going to make a personal appeal to my hon. friend to withdraw his amendment. He has brought the subject to the attention of the house; he has brought it to the attention of the country; and I ask him now in the interests of the country, the maintenance of national unity and the avoidance of religious controversy at this time of war that, having served his purpose by bringing up the subject, he ask leave of the house to withdraw his motion and not have the matter carried to a division. I shall give him and the house reasons why I feel the way I do, and what I think would be a preferable course to the one he has adopted.
While I was speaking with one hon. member this afternoon as to a previous vote, the vote on the motion moved by the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin), the hon. member mentioned to me that he thought that all the ex-minister had in mind was to bring the matter up for discussion, that he did not really mean any want of confidence in the government, but that it was perhaps the only chance he would get to present the point of view which he had presented. There may be some hon. members who are still of that impression with regard to the motion to which I have referred and some who may so view the present motion and other similar motions. May I point out that, on going into committee of supply, hon. members have the right to bring up for discussion any subject whatever if it is of the nature of a grievance. To bring forward a subject of grievance at the time of a motion to resolve the house into committee of supply does not mean that the matter has to be in the form of a motion or if in the form of a motion, pressed to a division.
If hon. members wish to bring a subject up in this house and have it discussed without subjecting the government to any expression of want of confidence they may bring the matter up on the motion to go into supply,
and if this is done by way of amendment when the proposed amendment has been discussed they may ask that the motion be withdrawn and that the house be permitted to go into committee of supply. That opportunity is open to hon. members and that is one way in which questions upon which hon. members wish to present their views can be presented even if they are of a most controversial character. But to dignify a question of this kind by treating it as something so important that it must be brought forward in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne in the form of a vote of want of confidence in the administration, seems to me to be not only the wrong way of proceeding but to be a course which helps to bring parliament itself into contempt in the eyes of the people.
The people of this country expect this parliament to get on with measures relating to the war. They are not looking to members of parliament moving amendment after amendment all in the nature of motions of want of confidence in the administration, once the house has tested the confidence or lack of confidence there may be in the ministry. The motion of the leader of the opposition is a test on that point, each amendment is a further test, but all these motions when they are moved on the address in this way are want of confidence motions, because they mean that if they should carry his excellency would not be thanked for his speech, a speech which set forth the policy of the government, and the whole policy of the government would be repudiated by the House of Commons. If hon. members appreciate the significance of proceedings of the house and the manner in which, according to parliamentary procedure, they should be conducted, they would have no difficulty in finding that this want of confidence motion should be voted down, if it comes to a vote.
But may I go a step further than that. The government I maintain has the right to ask every hon. member of this house if they are not prepared to give their support to the government in most things, that at least they will not seek to embarrass the government in its war effort. I ask my hon. friend, does he think that the motion which he has introduced to-night is in any way going to strengthen the hands of the government in seeking to maintain national unity in this country in this time of war? If he does not, I think he ought to be prepared to withdraw his amendment.
May I say to him that the government has considered what it is wisest to do with Mr. Shields. I want to put before him a side of the matter which perhaps he has not considered. I do not think it is part of the business

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
of the government to try to deal with matters of religious controversy. The first part of my hon. friend's amendment has the effect of blaming the government for not taking steps to stop what he terms "the present antiCatholic propaganda." That is one of the grounds on which his amendment is based, that the government should have taken steps to prevent anti-Catholic propaganda. When I said that the government had thought of what action it should take in regard to Mr. Shields it was not in connection with what he was doing in the way of anti-Catholic propaganda, it was in respect to one particular statement he had made which had relation to the defence of Canada regulations, and whether or not Mr. Shields should be prosecuted for what he had said in that connection. The hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) by a slip of the tongue, I think, said that if Mr. Shields was to be persecuted such and such a course should be taken. I think my hon. friend meant to say, if he was to be prosecuted.

speechtext:
Now there is the whole situation as related to the amendment of the hon. member for Gaspe. The government would have to consider whether it were best to risk making a martyr of Mr. Shields, give him an excuse for saying he was being persecuted, or whether it were better to leave matters of libel and slander to the courts of the country to be dealt with in accordance with the law of the land. The law of the land provides as the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) pointed out, that prosecutions in such matters are to be instituted by the attorney general of a province, not by the attorney general of the dominion. Let me ask my hon. friend this question-and I am putting the whole case before him and before the house and the country in order that all may see how I at least view' these matters. Assume that my colleague the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) who has been in the government just over a year I think, within the first few months of his coming into office, or at any time up to the present, had as Attorney General of Canada sought in some way to bring action against Mr. Shields in the province of Ontario, what would the cry have been all over this country? That the government at Ottawa, which had a large following from the province of Quebec, at the instance of its following from Quebec province, through its new Minister of Justice from Quebec province had started a prosecution on religious matters in the province of Ontario.

What situation would have followed from that. If you want to start a religious controversy in this country that it may be impossible to control, just begin having matters of the kind affecting race and religion dealt with as between one province and another.
The laws of libel and slander exist and to these laws recourse for redress may be had by churches as well as other institutions and by individuals. It is open to anyone to bring an action against Mr. .Shields for anything he says that is libelous. But as long as no individual brings an action against him, as long as the church itself or representatives of the church think it wiser not to bring action, because they do not wish to let him assume the role of a martyr and give more notoriety to a man who may be seeking notoriety and martyrdom above everything; so long as that step is not taken by the parties most interested I do not see why the government of Canada should be expected to take action to deal with religious controversy.
Turn the situation, around. What would be said of an effort by the government to stop, in one province, anti-protestant propaganda in another? Unfortunately, both among those who profess that they are in the communion of the Roman Catholic church and those who profess they are in the communion of the Protestant churches, there are men \vho to my mind have no right in this world to speak in the name of religion, who despite their professions, are intolerant and seek to stir up all the religious strife they possibly can. I think the common sense of the people deals in the end most effectively with those people. I do not think the people of Ontario take Mr. Shields as seriously as does my hon. friend from the province of Quebec. They know men, of that type, and they feel that the best way to deal with them is to ignore them, treat them with contempt. Speaking here as a member of a Protestant church, I wish to say that I have utter contempt for Mr. Shields and his unworthy utterances. I believe that the right-thinking men and women of our country share an equal contempt for the head of any church or one belonging to any denomination who tries to stir up in this country in time of war religious controversy and strife. If in these matters there is any action to be taken by any government the action should certainly be taken by the authorities of the province which is the proper one to deal with such matters.
I have dealt sufficiently I think with the point that I wished particularly to bring out.

The Address-Mr. Cardin
namely, how completely we would have misapplied the government's powers had we taken the course of action which my hon. friend says in his subamendment we should have taken. Instead of making a bad situation any better we would have made it infinitely worse.
I have said that there are other times at which this matter could more fittingly be dealt with. If the house wishes to have a further discussion with respect to Mr. Shields or any matter that has to do with religious controversy, then I say let us have one of our secret sessions and there discuss the matter as fully as we please. My hon. friend opposite smiles when I say, let us have a secret session

speechtext: I was not smiling at that. I would not dignify it with a secret session.

speechtext:
Well, my
reason for suggesting a secret session is that if there are any hon. members who feel deeply on these matters and want them discussed, I for one would be prepared to discuss them as fully as possible in any session of this parliament which would not create in this country a worse situation than it was being sought to remedy. A secret session, as I see it, is the only kind of session at which a matter of this sort could be properly dealt with in time of war. So I say to my hon. friend that if he withdraws his amendment and wishes to have this matter further discussed at a secret session, for my part I will be prepared to seek to meet his wishes by providing an opportunity for discussion in that way. But I do not think this debate should be continued longer, because every voice that is raised in discussion, on one side or the other, is only helping to create or foster religious controversy in Canada during this time of war. Since the beginning of this war I have done my utmost to prevent anything in the nature of political discussion of a serious controversial character from developing to a point where it would become a question of race or religion. If in time of war we ever get into a discussion of controversies that relate to matters of race and religion, then, we shall be handing this country over to the enemy without further fighting to save it.
So, Mr. Speaker, I hope my hon. friend will accept the suggestion I have offered and at least, if he cannot help the government, will not seek to embarrass us more than is necessary in our endeavour to carry on the war effort of the country.

I do not propose to make any extended remarks on the subamendment that
has been moved by the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Roy). While I sympathize with many of the points he has expressed during the presentation of his case, in all sincerity I must tell him that as the motion is framed I cannot support it, because it mixes religious questions with economic and political matters.
I agree with the hon. gentleman that there is necessity for a discussion of the subjects dealt with in his subamendment. Because we come from the province of Quebec there is no reason why we should not express our views on such questions and always be afraid of endangering national unit}'. We are not the only province responsible for the maintenance of national unity in Canada. We have our rights and privileges under the constitution, as have the citizens of every other province. We have the right, to which no one can object, to voice our views and our contentions on the floor of this house, and it is time we stopped trying to teach a lesson to the representatives of the province of Quebec only. Difficult questions affecting national unity are often raised by other representatives of the Canadian people in this House of Commons, but unfortunately the blame always falls upon the province of Quebec. We are always being asked to make sacrifices and to cease making representations because in the opinion of some our attitude might be interpreted as interfering with our war effort.
With that I cannot agree. I repeat that the motion presented by the hon. member for Gaspe deals with matters which we should be given an opportunity to discuss, and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has promised that such an opportunity will be provided. That opportunity should be given not only to the hon. member for Gaspe but to all other members of this house who have similar questions to raise.
I am not ready to support the subamendment, however, because it raises too many questions at the same time. The subamendment is a little too complicated, and a vote upon it would be almost unintelligible not only to this house but to the country. If an opportunity is given for discussion I would be ready to support the hon. member on many of the points he brought up in his remarks, whatever may be the criticism as to the length of time taken or the delay occasioned to the other business of the house. These matters are of importance, and we should have the right to discuss them freely and completely.
I am not entirely satisfied with the observations made by the Prime Minister. We are told that all our actions should be directed toward the winning of the war, that we should not do anything to embarrass or hinder what
The Address-Mr. St. Laurent

must be done by the government. If we are going to stop thinking; if we are going to cease taking any action in this house; if we are going to cease expressing any opinions which are not in agreement with the policies of the government, then we might just as well close parliament, go home and let the affairs of the country be administered by orders in council. We ought to be reasonable, I admit. We ought to take into consideration the position in which the government finds itself and the difficulties with which it has to contend. I am quite ready to do my share to help the government discharge its duties. But I am not ready to sacrifice the right to express my own view's on questions which I think are important and deserving of the attention of the members of the house.
The practice we are asked to follow here does not prevail anywhere except in Canada. If you look at the reports of proceedings in other parliaments you will see that members are free to discuss any question, that representatives are not met at every step with the objection that what they are doing may delay the progress of the war effort or may in some way embarrass the war policy of the government.
My motion was not made with that purpose at all. It was the logical conclusion of what had been said by all members having spoken in the debate.	I never asked that the
mobilization act should be suspended in its entirety. I asked that part of it only should be suspended for a short time, pending an investigation; that was all. My motion has been misrepresented and my words have been distorted during the debate.

I frankly admit the great responsibility which is on the government at the present time; I have never denied it. I have been ready up to now, as I will be ready from now on, to do the best I can to help, without going to the extent of trampling upon my own convictions. I am ready to do the best I can to help the government discharge its responsibilities, which I repeat are great; but I claim that on certain questions at least parliament has a right to express
fMr Cardin.]
its will, and that the representatives of the people in this house have a right to voice their disagreement with certain policies of the government. This is not unpatriotic. This is not doing anything against the united nations in their endeavour to win the war. It is merely preserving, even during war time, the privileges and liberties of the members of a democratic parliament, for which at the present time our armies are fighting.
If we are going to be prevented from expressing our views on any subject on account of the war, then I repeat that we might as well go home, and close up parliament, because there will be nothing left for us to do here.
Therefore I am not very much impressed by the argument that we should stop discussion on most subjects not directly related to the war, simply because it might be embarrassing to the government. I am not very much impressed, either, by the argument that if action had been taken against Pastor Shields by the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent), who is a French Canadian, it would have caused an upheaval all over the country. It could have caused trouble only in the minds of those who do not understand Canadian problems.
If there was cause for prosecution, whether the Minister of Justice is a French Canadian or an English-speaking Canadian, procedures should have been taken, without any fear or hesitation. The Minister of Justice, as such, must prosecute any man who does something contrary to the laws of the country. His action should not be influenced simply because he happens to belong to the minority.
But I concur in the opinion of the Prime Minister that at this time we should not mix religious matters with political and economic questions. And it is because I agree with that view expressed by the Prime Minister, that I join him in asking the hon. member for Gaspe to withdraw his motion, now that he has been given an opportunity of speaking on the subjects contained in his subamendment. I suggest to him, as a French Canadian, as a citizen of the province of Quebec, and as a man as deeply interested as he is in having our race and our religion respected in Canada, to make that little concession, reserving his right to discuss fully the matter on a more appropriate occasion.
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice): Mr. Speaker, before the debate goes any further may I point out that evidently the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin) has overlooked a provision in the British North America Act which a minister of justice cannot overlook, namely, that the

The Address-Mr. Coldwell
administration of justice is not only the privilege but is the responsibility of the attorneys general of the provinces respectively. Whenever anything requires to be done by the Attorney General of Canada the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres may be assured that so long as I am the Attorney General of Canada I will attempt to do it, no matter where it happens to be, no matter what race or creed may be affected, no matter what persons may be concerned.
But this matter, if it does constitute an offence constitutes such offence against the criminal law of the country, the administration of which is the responsibility of attorneys general of the provinces. It is not a war offence; it is not something contravening the regulations for the defence of Canada. If an offence has been committed along the lines suggested in the subamendment of the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Roy) it is an offence against peace-time law as much as it is against war-time law. And it possibly may be an offence, if in fact it does amount to sedition, under the common law of British countries. Sedition in British countries may consist of exciting ill-will between different classes of his majesty's subjects. But that raises a question of fact which must be determined by a court, according to the common law procedure of the country; and a prosecution can be brought about by anyone who will take the responsibility under oath of laying a complaint. Such complaint will be investigated, and if the investigating magistrate comes to the conclusion that a prima facie case has been made out, he will commit for trial. The case will then be the subject of a bill which, in due course, will be presented to his majesty's grand jury. If they in turn find a true bill the case will be brought before an ordinary court of justice. A jury will be empaneled and will determine the question whether the words or actions did amount to something which would excite ill-will between different classes of his majesty's subjects. That is as much a peace-time matter as a war-time matter, and as such is something which could be prosecuted by the attorney general of any province where the alleged offence was committed.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say only a word, following the remarks we have just heard, remarks which have disturbed me rather greatly. I suppose none of us wants to see any controversey raised of a religious or racial nature, and I think everything should be done to prevent anything of the kind from being fomented in the country in which we live at this particular time.
I was, however, rather alarmed at the statement just made by the Attorney General of Canada, the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent). The wide interpretation he gave respecting the laws of sedition and slander is such that if the government of Canada followed the line he laid down, then a government could constitute itself the judge of what should be said and what should not be said.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: No, no.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Yes, yes. That was surely implied in the remarks made by the Minister of Justice.
This is a British parliament. It is a parliament which operates under the greatest possible freedom of thought and the greatest possible freedom of speech. In my opinion it is a dangerous thing to interfere with freedom of thought or freedom of speech at any possible time and under any possible circumstances. In my opinion, if you interfere with freedom of thought or freedom of speech on the part of a certain individual to-day, you interfere with freedom of thought and speech of another individual to-morrow. And you gradually narrow down the range of that freedom in the country in which we live. Ultimately you arrive at something in the nature of a dictatorship.
Yesterday we were debating the defence of Canada regulations. The party with which I am associated stood for a principle. We have no association with the communist party. We have no association with the Jehovah's Witnesses, but yesterday we stood resolutely for the principle that under the British constitution and under British laws these people have the right to freedom of thought and freedom of speech. The same thing applies to every other religious and political organization in the dominion. I hold no brief for Doctor Shields; indeed in my opinion the doctrine which he is preaching has led to a
The Address-Division

dangerous feeling of disunity in this country. Every person ought to be aware of the danger that lies therein.
Let me say in passing that the party with which I am associated, although at times it has been subjected to religious condemnation, has never adopted similar tactics. We would never under any circumstances raise the issue of race or religion in this parliament or in this country. I appeal to my hon. friends on all sides of the house, of all races and of all religions, to accept as a principle in this parliament that we forgo any appeal to religious or racial prejudices. Let us live together in unity under the constitution and under the principles upon which this parliament has been founded, the principle of freedom of thought and the principle of freedom of speech, believing as we do that ultimately right and justice will prevail.
